bio.en: Jen Abel is co-founder of JJELLYFISH, where she helps early-stage founders learn to sell, and now GM of Enterprise at a high-growth company; this episode is the tactical follow-up to her first, on going from ~$1M to ~$10M ARR in enterprise sales.
bio.zh: Jen Abel 是 JJELLYFISH 的联合创始人，帮助早期创始人学会销售，如今在某高成长公司担任企业业务 GM；这期节目是她首期节目（如何从 0 到 100 万美元 ARR 的创始人式销售）的战术续集，聚焦如何从约 100 万做到约 1000 万美元 ARR 的企业销售。

summary.en: Jen goes deep on enterprise sales as a creative, relationship-driven art: sell to a gap and an opportunity, not just a problem; stop discounting to win deals (it signals buyers aren't bought in and fake product-market fit); and avoid becoming 'one of three' being tested, because differentiation is everything. She explains how enterprise deals get done through trust and mutual back-scratching, why she skips outbound sales tools (everyone pulls from the same databases) in favor of unconventional back-door approaches, and how to craft deals that make buyers want to move mountains for you. It's the most in-the-weeds enterprise-sales playbook you'll find for free.
summary.zh: Jen 深入剖析企业销售这门“创造性、以关系驱动”的艺术：卖的是“缺口”与“机会”，而不只是问题；别靠打折赢单（那说明买家并未真的心动，还会伪造产品市场契合的假象）；更要避免沦为你被拿去“三选一”测试的对象，因为差异化就是一切。她解释了企业交易如何通过信任与互相帮忙达成、为何她不用外呼销售工具（大家都在同一批数据库里），而改用非传统的“后门”打法，以及如何设计让买家愿意为你移山的交易。这是你能免费找到的最深入的企业销售实战手册。

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: You need to vision cast, you need to sell to a gap, don't sell to a problem. When you're selling to a leader, you need to be selling an opportunity. The market doesn't want to be sold to, they want to buy.
turns.zh: 你需要描绘愿景，你需要面向"差距"去销售，而不是面向"问题"去销售。当你向一位领导者销售时，你要卖的是一个机会。市场不想要被推销，他们想要主动购买。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Most founders would rather get 10, 10K deals than lose nine and get one 100K deal.

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: In the very early days, people will discount till the cows come home because they think that's the way to get a deal done. The best clients are not going to do that to you. If they're sitting there nickel-and-diming you, they're not fully bought in on what you're selling them.
turns.zh: 在很早的阶段，人们会无休止地打折，因为他们觉得这是做成交易的办法。但最优质的客户不会这样对你。如果他们坐下来跟你斤斤计较、一分一厘地压价，说明他们对你所卖的东西并没有真正认可。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It might be giving you a false sense of success and product market fit.
turns.zh: 这可能会给你一种虚假的成功感和产品市场契合的错觉。

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: As soon as you become a comparison, as soon as you become one of three that they're testing out, you've already sort of lost. It's all about differentiation. Here's what you will be able to do tomorrow because of how we're going to serve you today.
turns.zh: 一旦你变成"备选对比项"，一旦你变成他们正在测试的"三选一"之一，你其实就已经输了。关键在于差异化。因为今天我们会这样服务你，所以明天你将能做到这些。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Something else that you talk about is that enterprise sales is very creative.
turns.zh: 你提到的另一点是，企业级销售非常有创造性。

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: It's more of an art. It's all about deal crafting. It is a relationship you're building with someone. If they know they can call on you, people will turn over rocks for you. I have a client at a Fortune 10 company where I was like, "It's so important we get the deal done this year. Is that possible?" And she's like, "It's a tall order, but if it's going to help you, let's do it." These are how enterprise deals gets done. It's relationships.
turns.zh: 它更像一门艺术。核心在于如何"设计交易"。你是在和某个人建立一段关系。如果他们知道可以随时找你，人们会为你全力以赴去铺路。我在一家财富 10 强企业有位客户，当时我说："今年把这笔交易做成非常重要，有可能吗？"她说："这是个很高的要求，但如果能帮到你，那我们就做吧。"企业级交易就是这样达成的——靠的是关系。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What's kind of like the state of the art on go-to-market outbound tooling?
turns.zh: 目前在 GTM（进入市场）外联工具方面，最前沿的做法是什么样的？

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: I don't use a tool. The thing about AI tools is they're all pulling from the same databases. I want to email someone not in the database that's getting hit by a million folks. I want to take a back door in, not the front door where everyone else is trick or treating.
turns.zh: 我不用工具。AI 工具的问题在于，它们都从同样的数据库里抓取数据。我想发邮件给那些不在数据库里、没被千万人轰炸过的人。我想走后门进去，而不是走所有人都去"不给糖就捣蛋"的前门。

turns.speaker: Lenny

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: It's fascinating because if you ask someone to describe the mid-market, actually, if you ask someone to describe the enterprise, every single person has a different answer. It's either based off of revenue, it's either based off of market cap, it's based off of employee size, and I think a lot of people can get lost because selling to a hundred person organization is a radically different game than selling to a thousand person organization and there's no hybrid approach. (00:06:35): So the best way to think about it is you have small business which typically can be really powered by marketing, and then you have enterprise, which is typically going to be sales led. If you bucket them into these two very specific silos, it makes it much, much easier to understand what game you're playing. Now, when we talk about mid-market, I usually will say, "Are we talking about the upper end of small business or are we talking about the lower end of enterprise?" (00:07:04): And most people are usually saying the lower end of enterprise. And I say, "Great, know you're playing the enterprise game. Know the type of people you need to hire, the type of ACV they need because it makes it a lot easier than trying to have this middle ground that catches everything that doesn't distinctly define SMB and enterprise." So I say the mid-market doesn't exist because what is a mid-market hire? It's either low end enterprise or upper end SMB, and if you bleed those two games you're going to lose. They're so distinctly different. So that's kind of my theory on it.

turns.zh: 为了让大家明白我们在说什么，当你说"一线"的时候，怎么理解什么是"一线"比较好？

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: Tier one is like your Walmarts, your McDonald's, your NVIDIAs, your Tesla, your ExxonMobil, your UnitedHealthcare, the logos that are the leader in their space, their job is to stay in the number one spot.
turns.zh: 一线就是像沃尔玛、麦当劳、英伟达、特斯拉、埃克森美孚、联合健康这样的公司，也就是各自领域里的领导者，它们的任务就是保住第一的位置。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow. Your advice is because this is very counterintuitive. This is exactly what you're here not to do. Your advice is go after the Chevrons and the Mobils and the Walmarts as a startup.
turns.zh: 哇。你的建议真是……因为这非常反直觉。这恰恰是人们觉得初创公司不该做的事。你的建议是，作为一家初创公司，去追雪佛龙、美孚、沃尔玛这样的公司。

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: Because if you can get them, that's all the proof you need.
turns.zh: 因为如果你能拿下它们，那就是你需要的全部证明。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: How do you approach finding someone? Let's just get tactical there. Just like say you're going after Walmart. I know this is not a five-second answer, but just how would someone approach finding someone at Walmart to sell to?
turns.zh: 你是怎么找到对接人的？我们就具体一点。假设你要追沃尔玛。我知道这不是五秒钟能答完的，但一个人要怎么去找沃尔玛里可以销售的对象？

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: First of all, make sure the founder is involved, right? Everyone loves talking to a founder, so we'll start with let's get the founder involved as fast as human possible. The second is you need to vision cast, you need to sell to a gap, don't sell to a problem. There's a very big difference between problem selling and gap selling. Problem selling is highly specific, more technical than not, and it's the way that every salesperson is going to go about it, find the problem and anchor to it. (00:11:33): When you're selling to a leader, you need to be vision casting and you need to be selling an opportunity which is they are here, here's where we can take you. You know that image where it's like Mario or Mario, and then there's the mushroom and then there's Mario on blast, and everyone is like, "Don't sell the mushroom, sell Mario on blast." Well, that's exactly what it's saying. (00:11:57): It's about selling the opportunity. That's what gets the tier one logos excited and that is the best thing for a founder to sell, selling the vision versus the problem, and also it's what gets them to want to take a swing. Who wants to take a swing because you can do some small problem? They're not going to go to bath for that.
turns.zh: 首先，确保创始人亲自参与，对吧？每个人都喜欢和创始人聊，所以第一步就是让创始人以最快速度参与进来。第二，你需要描绘愿景，你需要面向"差距"去销售，而不是面向"问题"。问题式销售和差距式销售有天壤之别。问题式销售非常具体，多半偏技术，也是每个销售员都会采用的方式——找到问题并锚定它。(00:11:33)：当你向一位领导者销售时，你需要描绘愿景，你要卖的是一个机会：他们现在在这里，而我们可以带他们去到那里。你知道那张图吗——马里奥，然后有个蘑菇，然后是"火力全开"的马里奥，大家都在说："别卖蘑菇，要卖火力全开的马里奥。" 嗯，说的正是这个。(00:11:57)：它是关于卖机会。那才是让一线 logo 兴奋的东西，也是创始人最该卖的东西——卖愿景而不是卖问题，而且那也是让他们愿意试一把的原因。谁会因为你只能解决某个小问题就愿意试一把？他们不会为那种事去全力争取。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What's an example of a vision cast in a company you've worked with just to make this real? What does it look like when you've done a great job?
turns.zh: 能不能举一个你合作过的公司里"描绘愿景"的例子，让这更具体？当你做得特别好时，它是什么样子的？

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: We have an ability to deliver alpha, meaning, we have information, we have data, we have a way of working that no one else can do or is going to unlock a new way of thinking for you or an ability to deliver to a customer or an ability to solve a problem. Right now, you have an ability to access this level of information. I have an opportunity through our resources or through this gated data, we have access to get you much further upstream so that you can get information faster sooner. It's kind of like the high-frequency trading that one second, that one second. They didn't do much. They didn't sell, "Oh, we're doing fiber cable connectivity. We're giving you one second of alpha before everyone else." It's more of that ability and that's not problem-selling, that's opportunity selling.
turns.zh: 我们有能力提供 alpha，意思是，我们拥有信息、数据、一种别人做不到的工作方式，或者能为你开启一种全新的思维方式，或者能让你具备服务客户、解决问题的能力。现在，你已经能够接触到这一层级的信息。我有一个机会——通过我们的资源或通过这种受控数据——让我们能带你更往上游走，让你更快、更早地获取信息。这有点像高频交易里那一秒、那一秒。它们没做什么大事。它们不是卖"哦，我们在做光纤连接，我们比别人早一秒给你 alpha"。它更多是那种能力，而且那不是问题式销售，那是机会式销售。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I like this phrasing of just giving them alpha, that's such a simple way to imagine what this should feel like. We'll link to that image you're talking about with the Mario and-
turns.zh: 我喜欢"给他们 alpha"这个说法，这让人很容易想象那应该是什么感觉。我们会放上你提到的那张马里奥的图片链接——

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: You know that image?
turns.zh: 你知道那张图吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, the person that made that image originally is Kathy Sierra, if you remember her, do you remember? So there's this person, Kathy Sierra, she's from back in the day. This was a big, I don't know, lesson she taught is you want to not sell your people on a feature or a product. You want to sell them on them becoming a superhero.
turns.zh: 是的，最初做那张图的人是 Kathy Sierra，如果你记得她的话——你还记得吗？就是 Kathy Sierra，她是很早以前的人了。她教过一个很重要的——怎么说呢——道理：你不要向人们推销某个功能或产品，你要让他们相信自己能成为超级英雄。

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: Yeah, that's right.
turns.zh: 对，没错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: They are now a superhero because of the thing you've built for them. And so the vision here is here's how you become a superhero. Here's how this alpha will help you become more successful.
turns.zh: 因为你所打造的东西，他们现在成了超级英雄。所以这里的愿景就是：你如何成为超级英雄。这个 alpha 会如何帮你变得更成功。

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: And that's why founders are so good at selling because they naturally go to vision selling and vision casting versus a typical trained salesperson is find the problem, ask these questions and it just kills the vibe. It just feels like you're talking to a salesperson, right? (00:14:08): It's like, "What's your script? And it's like that's not vision selling, that's like playbook selling." And in the age of AI where a lot of it is Alpha, it's about speed, it's about getting access to information, it's about training data, and look at how the market is reacting to it. It's all opportunity and it's all about the alpha.
turns.zh: 这就是为什么创始人特别擅长销售，因为他们天然就会去做愿景式销售和描绘愿景，而典型的受过训练的销售员则是：找问题、问这些问题，结果把氛围全毁了。就感觉你是在跟一个销售员说话，对吧？(00:14:08)：就像，"你的话术是什么？" 那不是愿景式销售，那是"剧本式销售"。在 AI 时代，很多东西都是 alpha，讲究的是速度、是获取信息的渠道、是训练数据，看看市场是怎么反应的——全都是机会，全都是 alpha。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So just to make this more concrete for people, Sam, like sales person at Cursor, what would be an example of vision casting? The obvious idea there is your team will be more productive, you'll get more done faster than everybody else. Is that a big enough vision to cast?
turns.zh: 为了让大家更具体一点，假设 Sam 是 Cursor 的销售员，描绘愿景的例子会是什么？最显而易见的想法是"你的团队会更高产，你会比所有人都更快完成更多事"。这个愿景够大吗？

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: I think it may be more of you'll be able to actually hire the 10X engineers that you don't necessarily have access to because they want to be able to use this type of tool. It's about letting them get differentiated talent or that's probably more of what I would anchor to of this is the 10X engineers use cursor. You don't, do you want access to 10X engineers?
turns.zh: 我觉得更像是：你将能真正招到那些你本来接触不到的 10 倍工程师，因为他们想用这类工具。关键是让他们能招到差异化的人才，或者——我更可能锚定这一点——10 倍工程师都用 Cursor。你不想接触 10 倍工程师吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: They won't even join your company if you're not using Cursor.
turns.zh: 如果你不用 Cursor，他们根本不会加入你的公司。

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: Yeah, yeah. Think about it. So many people are so specific about what they're able to, I think especially technical folks, I'm not a technical person, but I would imagine that they're not going to go to, they don't like to go to these corporations because they're forced to use some incumbent tools.
turns.zh: 对，对。想想看。很多人——我觉得尤其是技术人——对能用的工具特别挑剔，我不是技术人，但我猜他们不会去、也不喜欢去那些公司，因为被迫要用某些既有的工具。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Going back to going after these larger companies, I asked your colleague, Justin, what he sees you do that most impacts the success that teams have with their sales process. And there's a bunch of I'm going to touch on, but one is most founders are insecure about asking for large ACVs for charging, or the way he put it is most founders would rather get 10 10K deals than lose nine and get one 100K deal. Talk about your advice there and what you see.
turns.zh: 回到追这些大公司的话题，我问过你的同事 Justin，他看到你做的哪些事最能影响团队销售流程的成功。这方面有好几点我要讲到，其中一点是：大多数创始人对索要高额 ACV（平均合同金额）收费感到心虚，或者像他说的——大多数创始人宁愿拿 10 个 1 万的单，也不愿丢掉 9 个、只换来 1 个 10 万的单。聊聊你在这方面的建议和观察。

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: There are in the very early days is people will discount till the cows come home because they think that's the way to get a deal done. The best clients are not going to do that to you because that's like a qualification criteria, which is like if they're sitting there nickel-and-diming you being like, "No, I don't believe it's worth this. I don't believe it's worth that." They're not fully bought in on what you're selling them. (00:16:32): So when I say I'd rather get $100,000 deal than $10,000 deals, I'd rather have one rock star client that's going to help me figure out the next stage of where this is going than 10 or maybe five that are a good fit, five that are not, and I still have to serve those five that are not a good fit, and that's going to distract me. So this is why I love enterprise sales is they're not going to do the hard work of bringing you in if it's not critical or if it's not, when I say critical, it's going to impact them in a way that they're going to make it successful, that's what I love about enterprise sales. (00:17:14): They have the resources to ensure that it gets implemented because most in today's day and age, if people are not using the tool, you just get rid of the tool. So they're going to want to make sure whatever they bring in, what they go to bat for, remember, they go to bat once every two years, maybe once every three years. You've got to make it feel incredible. You've got to make it feel like they're going to be a superhero going back to it. (00:17:42): Otherwise, what's the point? Because the way enterprises are structured is it is designed today to make it hard to buy because they want to make sure whatever you're bringing in, you really, really want it gets rid of the mediocre. I think this would be good and it gets to this is going to change the way we work. It's going to impact our ability to capture some form of alpha, however you want to define that for them and it's sticky because of that.
turns.zh: 在很早的阶段，人们会无休止地打折，因为他们觉得这是做成交易的办法。但最优质的客户不会这样对你，因为这就像一条筛选标准：如果他们坐下来跟你斤斤计较，说"不，我觉得这不值这个价，我觉得那不值那个价"，说明他们对你卖的东西并没有真正认可。(00:16:32)：所以我说我宁愿要一笔 10 万美元的单，也不要 10 笔 1 万美元的单——我宁愿要一个能帮我搞清楚下一步往哪走的明星客户，也不要 10 个（或者 5 个合适、5 个不合适）客户，而我还要去服务那 5 个不合适的，那只会分散我的精力。这就是为什么我喜爱企业级销售：如果一件事不关键，他们是不会费那么大劲把你引进门的；我说"关键"，是指它会以某种方式影响他们、让他们把它做成，这正是我热爱企业级销售的原因。(00:17:14)：他们有资源确保落地，因为在今天这个时代，如果人们不用这个工具，你就直接被弃用了。所以他们会想确认，任何他们引进、为之全力争取的东西——记住，他们大概两三年才全力争取一次——必须让人感觉惊艳。必须让他们感觉自己会因此成为超级英雄，回到这一点上。(00:17:42)：否则有什么意义？因为企业的组织结构，今天就是设计成"让你很难买"的，因为他们想确认你真的、真的想要它，从而筛掉平庸的东西。我觉得"这个应该不错"是不够的，要让人觉得"这会改变我们的工作方式"。它会提升我们获取某种 alpha 的能力——无论你怎么为他们定义 alpha——而且正因为如此，它才具有粘性。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So your advice here broadly is don't pay attention to the smaller 10K-ish kind of opportunities for a bunch of reasons. One is it might be giving you a false sense of success in product market fit. Two, those companies are maybe not as innovative and won't lead you in the right direction. Three are probably discounts just like your product than your pricing just gets thrown off.
turns.zh: 所以你这边的整体建议是，不要去关注那些 1 万左右的小机会，原因有好几个。一是它可能给你一种虚假的成功感和产品市场契合的错觉。二是那些公司可能没那么创新，不会把你引向正确的方向。三是它们多半会要求打折，结果你的产品定价就全乱了。

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: Yep, and also you don't really get taken seriously for 10K. You get way more taken seriously for a 100Ks, it's much harder to get a 100K deal done and an executive use needs to be involved. I'd much rather have an executive sign-off on something and spend two more months getting the deal done because you know that they are bought in, you can now ensure what kind of value do they want to unlock and maybe you have an opportunity to turn them into a user, which to me, in today's day and age, with our generation being the ones that are now the executives at these corporations, this is native to them.
turns.zh: 对，而且 1 万美元的单你真的不被当回事。10 万美元的单才会被认真对待，而且做成 10 万的单难得多，需要高管参与。我宁愿让一位高管对某件事签字批准，再多花两个月把交易做成，因为你知道他们是真的认可了，你现在能确认他们想解锁什么样的价值，而且也许有机会把他们变成用户——对我来说，在今天这个时代，我们这一代人正是这些公司里的高管，这对他们来说是与生俱来的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Who is this true for? Is the advice here basically, if you're trying to build a successful B2B company, everybody should be aiming towards these a 100K sort of deals? Is there a world where you can be successful with 10Ks for a long time?
turns.zh: 这对谁适用？这里的核心建议是不是说，如果你想做一家成功的 B2B 公司，每个人都应该瞄准那种 10 万美元级别的交易？有没有可能你长期靠 1 万美元的单也能成功？

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: If you have a super high win rate in a massive market, because all you have to do is reverse engineer the math. If you need to generate a hundred million dollars in revenue, how many 10K deals do you need? And the expansion on a 10K deal is in parallel to that. Where can you go? 10 to 15? That's a 50% growth, much easier to go to a 100K to 500K because they want more bodies or they want more value out of you. (00:19:58): For an enterprise, they'd love to get more out of an existing customer. You're already trusted. So it's also about the type of company you are. If you're venture-backed, you can't be selling $10,000 deals to the enterprise, you'll get killed, or you've already lost the game because you're playing a small business game in the wrong sector.
turns.zh: 如果你在一个巨大的市场里有超高的赢单率，因为你要做的只是把数字倒推出来。如果你需要创造 1 亿美元营收，你得做多少个 1 万的单？而 1 万的单的增购空间也与之相当。你能涨到哪？1 万到 1.5 万？那是 50% 的增长，而做到 10 万涨到 50 万要容易得多，因为他们想要更多席位，或者想要你提供更多的价值。(00:19:58)：对企业来说，他们很乐意从现有客户身上获得更多。你已经被信任了。所以这也要看你是一家什么样的公司。如果你拿了风投，你不能给企业卖 1 万美元的单，你会被击垮，或者说你已经输了，因为你在错误的领域里打小企业的牌。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Have you seen startups you've worked with succeed in that 10K, 20K bucket or is it really, really rare?
turns.zh: 你有没有见过你合作过的初创公司在 1 万、2 万这个区间取得成功？还是说这真的非常非常罕见？

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: If they're going after the enterprise?
turns.zh: 你是说如果他们追的是企业级？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: Yes, if it's the first three months and then after three months, it turns into a 50K and then a 100K and it ramps up quickly. Sure, that makes sense. You got your foot in the door and you can expand it exponentially in a healthy manner. I think that that's fine. $10,000 a year, then going to 12, then going to 15, the math will break.
turns.zh: 是的，如果前三个月是这样，三个月后变成 5 万，然后变成 10 万，并且快速爬升，那当然说得通。你先挤进门，然后以健康的方式指数级扩张。我觉得那样没问题。一年 1 万，然后到 1.2 万，再到 1.5 万，这个数学就撑不住了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is great. I feel like most founders to this are like, "No, no, we're kind of in that exception we'll be all right. 10K, we'll do 20K. That's crazy to consider 100K."
turns.zh: 说得好。我觉得大多数创始人面对这个都会说："不不，我们大概是个例外，我们会没事的。1 万，我们做到 2 万。考虑 10 万也太离谱了。"

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: Yeah, the math will break. And also, a really good salesperson, you're commissioned on a 10K deal, they're not going to get a great salesperson. They're going to want to be anchored to how can I sell a $250,000 deal? How can I sell a half a million dollar deal? That's the type of person you want.
turns.zh: 对，数学会撑不住。而且，一个真正好的销售员，如果提成是按 1 万的单算，你根本招不到优秀的销售。他们会想锚定在"我怎么卖出 25 万的单？我怎么卖出 50 万的单？"那才是你想要的人。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And a big part of this is this is a good lens to force you to build the product that you can sell for 100K, 500K.
turns.zh: 而且这里很关键的一点是：这是个很好的视角，逼着你去打造一款能卖 10 万、50 万的产品。

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: Yeah, absolutely. And again, this is about playing that enterprise game. If you're trying to sell, if you're a small business, if you're in the small business place and an enterprise company comes to you and is like, "I like this." Ensure that you structure it for an enterprise. Don't play the small business team with an enterprise company.
turns.zh: 对，绝对是。再说一遍，这就是在打企业级的牌。如果你在卖，如果你是小企业，处在小企业的位置，而一家企业级公司来找你说"我喜欢这个"，那你要确保按企业级的结构来安排。别用小企业的团队去应付一家企业级公司。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Talk more about that. What does that mean?
turns.zh: 再多讲讲。这是什么意思？

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: Let's say you're PLG, and a big company like Walmart comes to and is like, "Hey, can we get access for three of our users?" And they're like, "This is so exciting." And then they sell them the small business pricing for three users to Walmart. Very, very hard now to go from those three users that you just priced them at in a small business way, turn that into 100K because now it's documented what they're actually paying for this. (00:22:08): So you're stuck. You've kind of anchored yourself to this price. Not to mention how are you going to unlock the executive high level value so that you can get that senior executive to buy in and stamp this as well. Otherwise, it's just going to be throwing it on the credit card. But again, you've just ruined your enterprise game because you're anchoring to a small business price. (00:22:34): So this is why when you bleed these two games, it's very, very, very dangerous because these are really smart companies. They're going to say, "Well, wait a second, I just paid $9,000 last year and now you want to charge me $90,000. Well, what's the step change in value? What's the 10X value I'm now getting?" That's super hard to prove.
turns.zh: 假设你做的是 PLG（产品驱动增长），像沃尔玛这样的大公司来找你说："嘿，我们能给三个用户开通吗？"然后他们很兴奋。结果你按小企业的定价把三个用户的席位卖给了沃尔玛。现在，要让你刚用小企业方式定价的这三个用户变成 10 万，就非常非常难了，因为他们的实际付费已经被记录下来了。(00:22:08)：所以你被卡住了。你某种程度上已经把自己锚定在这个价格上了。更别说你怎么去解锁高管层面的高价值，好让那位高级高管认可并盖章。否则，就只是把它扔到信用卡上付掉。但你又因此毁掉了自己的企业级打法，因为你锚定的是一个小企业价格。(00:22:34)：所以这就是为什么把这两套游戏混在一起非常非常非常危险，因为这些公司非常聪明。他们会说："等等，我去年才付了 9000 美元，现在你要收我 9 万？那价值的阶跃变化在哪？我现在得到的 10 倍价值是什么？" 那极难证明。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So the tip here is your initial price will really screw you if you get it wrong. And so obviously we're not going to give people the answer on their pricing strategy fully, but just is the advice just charged more or what would you recommend?
turns.zh: 所以这点的提示是：如果你的初始定价搞错了，会真的把你坑惨。我们显然不会把定价策略的答案完整给人，但这里的建议就是"多收钱"吗，还是你有什么推荐？

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: It is enterprise companies are very used to a land, when I say the first initial contract, somewhat between 75K and 150K, very used to that. In fact, that's probably where you want to start because you also want to understand where can you grow from this. Start contained, don't say 150K and sell the farm. Say, "It's 150K, here's who gets access, here's the value we're going to deliver and here's where we're going over time." You also want them to know, "Here's what we plan to do roughly in year two, year three." (00:23:42): I know it's hard to look that far out, but plant the seed with them in terms of where this is going. If you come in at $10,000, even if they want to bring you in and want to spend 100K with you, they have to be able to defend that and now they see a $10,000, it can get really messy, especially because a lot of them are using AI now to understand contracts. So they're going to quickly say, "Oh wait, you spent a thousand dollars with Lenny and now Lenny is asking you for a 100K. Great. Just help me understand why or defend it."
turns.zh: 是这样的：企业级公司非常习惯"land（初始切入）"——我说的是第一份初始合同——大致在 7.5 万到 15 万之间，他们非常习惯这个区间。事实上，那大概就是你该起步的地方，因为你也想知道从哪里能继续增长。起步要有节制，别一上来就说 15 万然后把全部都卖了。要说："这是 15 万，这是谁能使用，这是我们要交付的价值，以及我们随着时间会走到哪。"你也要让他们知道："这是我们大致在第二年、第三年打算做的事。"(00:23:42)：我知道看那么远很难，但要在他们心中种下这趟旅程会去哪里的种子。如果你从 1 万美元进来，即使他们想引进你、想跟你花 10 万，他们也得能为这个决定辩护；而现在他们看到的是 1 万，这会变得非常混乱，尤其是因为他们中很多人现在用 AI 来理解合同。所以他们很快就会说："哦等等，你跟 Lenny 花了 1000 美元，现在 Lenny 跟你要 10 万。很好。帮我理解一下为什么，或者帮我辩护一下。"

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I could totally see ChatGPT being like, "This is interesting."
turns.zh: 我完全能想象 ChatGPT 会说："这很有意思。"

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: Yeah, exactly.
turns.zh: 对，没错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It used to be 1K, now it's a 100K. What might be going on here?
turns.zh: 以前是 1 千，现在是 10 万。这里到底发生了什么？

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: Totally. The people don't realize how, again, know the game you're playing and don't be sloppy about it.
turns.zh: 完全如此。人们没意识到——再说一遍——要清楚自己在玩什么游戏，而且别马虎对待。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So your advice here is really interesting. There's the land to expand. Expand is very important, but the landing may screw your expanding because it sets the wrong reference point.
turns.zh: 所以你这个建议真的很有意思。有"先切入再扩张"。扩张很重要，但切入可能会毁掉你的扩张，因为它设下了一个错误的参照点。

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: 1,000%. That's exactly right. You said it better than I did.
turns.zh: 百分之百。完全正确。你说得比我好。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And so you may see in theory if you land a 10K go to 100K, that's an amazing NRR, everyone's going to be really impressed. But you're saying people won't buy into that. It's going to feel absurd and wrong.
turns.zh: 所以从理论上看，如果你从 1 万切入涨到 10 万，那是非常亮眼的 NRR（净收入留存率），所有人都会印象深刻。但你的意思是人们不会买账。这会让人觉得荒谬、不对劲。

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: Unless it's defendable. All it needs to be is defendable. But who can really defend? That's very hard to defend a 10X. 10X jump, they're going to want to see 15X value.
turns.zh: 除非它是可辩护的。它只需要是可辩护的就行。但谁真的能辩护？要辩护 10 倍很难。10 倍的跳跃，他们会想看到 15 倍的价值。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let's talk about design partners.
turns.zh: 我们来聊聊设计合作伙伴（design partners）。

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: Oh yeah.
turns.zh: 哦好啊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is something most founders try to do. They find a few folks to work with, to help them build the thing. What's your advice on when to start finding design partners? How to find design partners, what a good relationship looks like?
turns.zh: 这是大多数创始人都会尝试做的事。他们找几个人合作，帮他们把东西做出来。关于什么时候开始找设计合作伙伴、怎么找、好的合作关系是什么样的，你有什么建议？

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: Design partners are incredible. They're the hardest logos to upsell, meaning go from design partner to full rollout customer. So don't expect these people to be your million dollar pipeline. Expect these people to be the guide, to help you understand, maybe design partners could be a technology company in the Fortune 1,000. (00:25:50): So they're used to experimenting. They're used to technology, they're used to, they were once a startup, so they get it. Those make really good design partners. Most of the design partners that I've closed are usually technology based. They get it and they also are excited about advancing the org and also giving the team an ability to have that startup feel. (00:26:12): So if you're a large massive corporation like Stripe. Stripe doesn't get that startup vibe as much like that 50 person startup vibe, but this can be a gift to give them that lens and give them that voice and give them that excitement that they don't get as a larger company. But those are great types of logos to be early design partners because one, they want to make sure they continue to stay on the cutting edge, but two is they are, to try and build something without that guidance is really, really, really hard because they're not using it. (00:26:54): So you need that user feedback and you also need to tie that to the executive value. It's actually a lot, it's very hard to do, but if you can come out of it and upsell a design partner to a full rollout customer, such a huge win for the market for you, for your team, and also for your investors because it's the hardest customer to actually truly convert. (00:27:23): They've been it when it was messy, they usually got a low price point. But if you again frame it, say, "Listen, I would love for you to be a design partner. I want a little skin in the game to get you to point it. Here's where we want to go and you'll get a discount because you were in the beginning, but I'm setting the framing. Here's where we want to go with pricing. Here's where we are today. You'll always have 30% concession in perpetuity because you are there with us on day one." (00:27:49): So again, it's not about asking for $10,000 and then not expecting that design partner to upsell and keep it flat because there's no growth there. It's a flat. It's about getting that early design partner, set the framing, own the framing and let them know where you're going. Again, a $100,000 to these large logos if they want it, it's very easy for them to get it in.
turns.zh: 设计合作伙伴非常了不起。他们是最难增售（upsell）的 logo，也就是从设计合作伙伴变成全面铺开的客户。所以别指望这些人成为你百万美元的销售管道。要指望这些人当向导，帮你理解——也许设计合作伙伴可以是财富 1000 强里的一家科技公司。(00:25:50)：所以他们习惯做实验。他们习惯技术，他们习惯——他们曾经也是初创公司，所以懂这套。这些是非常好的设计合作伙伴。我签下的设计合作伙伴大多数都是偏技术的。他们懂，而且他们对推动组织前进、给团队一种初创公司的感觉感到兴奋。(00:26:12)：所以如果你是一家像 Stripe 这样的大公司。Stripe 不太有那种初创氛围，就是 50 人创业公司的那种氛围，但这可以是一个礼物——给他们那种视角、那种声音、那种他们在更大的公司里得不到的兴奋感。但这些是非常好的早期设计合作伙伴类型，因为第一，他们想确保自己持续站在前沿；第二，如果没有那种指引，他们要尝试去构建什么东西真的非常非常非常难，因为他们根本不用它。(00:26:54)：所以你需要那种用户反馈，你也需要把它和高管价值绑定。这其实很多、很难做，但如果你能做到，并把一个设计合作伙伴增售成全面铺开的客户，那对市场对、对你、对你的团队、对你的投资者都是一个巨大的胜利，因为这是最难真正转化的客户。(00:27:23)：他们是在一团乱的时候就在的，通常拿的是低价。但如果你再次定好框架，说："听我说，我很希望你能成为设计合作伙伴。我要你也在里面下一点注，好让你把它推起来。这是我们要去的方向，因为你是最早的，你会得到折扣，但框架是我来定的。这是我们在定价上要去的方向。这是我们今天的位置。你将永远享有 30% 的永久让利，因为你第一天就和我们在一起。"(00:27:49)：所以再说一遍，这不在于开口要 1 万美元，然后又不指望那个设计合作伙伴增售、让它一直持平，因为那里没有增长。它是平的。关键在于拿到那个早期设计合作伙伴，定好框架、掌控框架，并让他们知道你要去哪。再说一遍，对这些大 logo 来说，10 万美元只要他们想要，他们很容易批下来。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's this really interesting underlying piece of advice of finding a company that pulls you in the direction that leads to success. A company that's kind of a visionary. There's the obvious companies that everyone is always trying to get these days, OpenAI and Anthropic and Stripe I think is one. And any advice for just picking the right early? What are signs that this is a company that will point you in the right direction?
turns.zh: 这里有个非常有趣的底层建议：找一家能把你拉向成功方向的公司。一家有远见的公司。现在大家都一直在抢的那些明显的公司，OpenAI、Anthropic，还有 Stripe，我觉得算一个。关于选对早期（合作伙伴）有什么建议？有什么迹象表明这是一家会把你指向正确方向的公司？

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: I think they have to be part of a logo that is deemed startup-friendly or in that world, and then I think it's the person, is this person excited to give feedback? Does this person buy in to where we're going? Do they see this world differently like us? Are they in lockstep with the founder vision? (00:28:58): Are they excited to use a tool that's janky? Because it is janky in the beginning, but they know that where this can go can be incredible. So I think it's really about the person and making sure that they're aligned for what they're getting into, and I think a lot of salespeople oversell it. I think that's a common thing that happens and that leads to churn, that leads to frustration, that leads to sometimes just canceling the contract.
turns.zh: 我觉得他们得属于一家被视为对初创友好的 logo，或者说在那个圈子里；然后我觉得关键在人——这个人是否乐于给反馈？这个人是否认可我们要去的方向？他们是否像我们一样用不同的眼光看这个世界？他们是否和创始人的愿景步调一致？(00:28:58)：他们是否愿意用一个还很粗糙（janky）的工具？因为一开始确实是粗糙的，但他们知道它能去到的地方可以非常惊人。所以我觉得关键真的在人，要确保他们对自己要参与的事是认同的；而且我觉得很多销售员过度推销了。我觉得这是常发生的事，会导致流失、导致挫败，有时甚至直接导致取消合同。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: They oversell the initial kind of design partners phase over the product.
turns.zh: 他们把最初的设计合作伙伴阶段、也就是产品本身，给过度推销了。

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: They sell everything. Yeah, design partner, even full rollout, and it's so, so important to tell them, "Here's where we are today. Here's what we cannot do." Which is just as important. It builds trust. "Here's what we will allow you to do in the next six months. Do you want to be on this journey with us? And it's really ugly right now." Right? "Barely anything exists, but we would love your voice to be a part of it."
turns.zh: 他们什么都卖。对，设计合作伙伴，甚至全面铺开，而非常非常重要的一点是告诉他们："这是我们今天的位置。这是我们做不到的事。" 这同样重要。它建立信任。"这是未来六个月我们能让你做的事。你想和我们一起走这段旅程吗？现在真的很难看。" 对吧？"几乎什么都没有，但我们很希望有你的声音参与进来。"

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: One of the biggest fears I think founders have is having a company pull, basically build just for their use case and then it ends up not being used by a lot of people. And so how far do you go fixing their specific problems? Any advice on just how far to go with one company?
turns.zh: 我觉得创始人最大的恐惧之一，就是被一家公司牵着走，基本上只为他们自己的用例去构建，结果最后没多少人用。那你究竟要在解决他们具体问题上走多远？关于跟一家公司走多远，有什么建议？

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: That is the founder's job. The founder's job is to have a clear vision and do not let anything delineate from that. It's important to take feedback in terms of what is the market's reality, but it is the founder, and this is why being a founder is so hard. It is the founder's job to interpret that because a lot of feedback you get is this is the old way, they're responding this way because it's the old way of working. (00:30:37): They want you to build this because that's how they're traditionally expecting to do that. It is not, "Here's where we're going, this is why we're not doing that. I hear you, but here's why we're not going to do that because we're going to completely change the way you do this." That is the founder's job. (00:30:53): And I think we did a bunch of design partnerships late last year and there was a lot of feedback given, a lot of feedback given, but the founder had such clarity with where he wanted to go that he was like 80% noise, 20% had I not asked this question, I wouldn't have gotten that gold in terms of where they are today. And it's that 80/20 rule where 80% of what they're going to tell you is probably going to be not related to where you want to go or based off of the old way, but that 20% of, "Oh, I did not think about it that way." That drives everything.
turns.zh: 那是创始人的工作。创始人的工作是有清晰的愿景，并且不让任何东西偏离它。听取关于市场现实的反馈很重要，但解读这些反馈是创始人的事——这也是做创始人之所以难的原因。很多你得到的反馈是基于老一套，他们这样回应是因为那是老的工作方式。(00:30:37)：他们想让你构建这个，因为传统上他们就期望那样做。正确的做法不是这样，而是："这是我们去的方向，这就是为什么我们不做那个。我听到了，但这里是我不打算做那个的原因，因为我们要彻底改变你做这件事的方式。" 那是创始人的工作。(00:30:53)：我觉得我们去年底做了一批设计合作，给了很多反馈，非常多反馈，但那位创始人对自己要去哪有极其清晰的判断，他说 80% 是噪音，20% 是——如果我不问这个问题，我就得不到今天他们所在位置的那块金子。这就是 80/20 法则：他们告诉你的 80% 很可能跟你想去的方向无关，或者基于老一套，但那 20% 的"哦，我没想到可以那样想"，驱动了一切。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Have you seen a design partner pull a company in the wrong direction? Just screw their path? Have you seen that or is that pretty rare?
turns.zh: 你有没有见过设计合作伙伴把一家公司拉向错误的方向？把他们的路带偏？你见过吗，还是说相当罕见？

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: No, I don't think it's that rare. We hear people complain about it all the time, but I think it's more of an excuse.
turns.zh: 不，我觉得没那么罕见。我们一直听到有人抱怨这个，但我觉得那更多是个借口。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Coming back to this question of going after the enterprise versus SMBs. And again, early advice you gave is there's no, don't go in between. Either pick SMB small company, which I know you said there's a million ways to differentiate what this means, but I guess I think of employee numbers under some number over a thousand is maybe enterprise. Is that a good way to think about it just like-
turns.zh: 回到追企业级还是 SMB 这个问题。再说一遍，你早先的建议是：没有中间地带，别走中间。要么选 SMB 小公司——我知道你说过区分这个有很多方式——但我猜我会把员工数低于某个数、高于一千的算作企业级。这样想可以吗，比如——

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: Yeah, it depends. Are you selling per seats or are you selling based off of usage or are you selling off of, I think it also depends on the pricing model a little bit. I look at headcount too because it's just such an easy way to think about it because you can also gauge usage off that and a bunch of other things, but sometimes the small companies, I think we're going to see a lot more larger companies become smaller because of AI, not significantly smaller, but also high margins allow them to experiment more too.
turns.zh: 对，看情况。你是按席位卖、按用量卖，还是按别的卖？我觉得这也多少取决于定价模式。我也会看员工人数，因为这只是个容易理解的思考方式，而且你也能据此衡量用量和其他一些东西；但有时候小公司——我觉得我们会看到更多大公司因为 AI 而变小，不是显著变小，但高利润也让他们能更多地做实验。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's such an interesting point you're making there that the way we designate enterprise versus SMB like may shift because number of employees may go down with AI.
turns.zh: 你这里提出了一个非常有趣的点：我们区分企业级和 SMB 的方式可能会改变，因为员工数可能会随着 AI 下降。

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: Yeah. Oh yeah.
turns.zh: 对。哦没错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So interesting. So where I was going to go with this question is when people are deciding, I'm going to go enterprise versus I'm going to sell to startups, like YC companies are the typical example they sell to their own YC batches and you just broad advice of picking, "Okay, we go enterprise versus no, let's actually go startup."
turns.zh: 太有意思了。所以我这个问题本来想说的是：当人们做决定时，是要走企业级，还是要卖给初创公司——比如 YC 公司就是典型，他们卖给自己的 YC 批次——你有什么宽泛的建议来帮人选择："好，我们走企业级"，还是"不，我们其实去卖初创公司"？

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: I think it's about, and I read this somewhere and I wholeheartedly agree with it because I've seen it live. I think it's about what game does the founder best understand? Are they an incredible marketer and have some competitive edge for how they can win a massive audience? (00:33:34): I would say go SMB and marketing led or are they a bit more really understand how large corporations work and really excited to deliver on $100,000 plus type of opportunities or the value that they are building for is way more relatable to an enterprise versus a small business.
turns.zh: 我觉得这取决于——我在某处读到过这个，而且我完全认同，因为我亲眼见过。我觉得这取决于创始人最理解哪套游戏？他们是不是一位出色的营销者，在如何赢得庞大受众上有某种竞争优势？(00:33:34)：我会说那就走 SMB、走营销驱动；还是说他们更懂大公司是怎么运作的，并且对交付 10 万美元以上级别的机会感到真正兴奋，或者他们正在构建的价值对企业级来说远比对小公司更有共鸣。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is really interesting. I've never heard of it described that way. I think about linear, which started very startup-ey and my take is they did that because changing the way you work is really hard and their bet was like, "Let's start with companies and grow with them and over time that becomes the default." Any reaction to that?
turns.zh: 这真的很有意思。我从没听过这样描述。我想到 Linear，它一开始非常"创业感"，我的理解是他们这么做是因为改变工作方式真的很难，他们的赌注是："从公司开始，和它们一起成长，久而久之这就成了默认。" 对此有什么看法？

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: I think that it sounds like that that's a great way to work because that's a technical tool, so that you need the right, also need to have the right infrastructure to sell. I think Slack, look, Slack and Microsoft Teams are still battling it out at the enterprise. turns.zh: 我觉得这听起来是个很好的运作方式，因为那是个技术工具，所以你需要对的——也需要有对的销售基础设施。我觉得 Slack，看，Slack 和 Microsoft Teams 在企业级还在激烈竞争。我觉得这也关乎你怎么接入、怎么集成，以及他们到底有没有对的系统来支持你？OpenAI 的优势在于他们不需要连接任何东西。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Say more about that.
turns.zh: 再多讲讲这个。

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: So the value, people were bringing their own use cases to it and it's not like they, well they can ingest and they built that, it's a brand new thing and they started I think, this is someone told me this, so this could be hearsay, but I believe that they were already speaking to CTOs even well before they released to help them explain where this is all going and get their buy-in. (00:35:17): And it's much easier to get into the enterprise when you're like, "We won't even touch your data, won't even touch your data. (00:35:41): So you have to start small and low risk, which is like, "Hey, what is the subset of consumers that churned? Let's figure out how we could have made them happier, whatever it be." So that data is lower risk. So again, it's also understanding your market and understanding what their ability to experiment is.
turns.zh: 所以价值在于，人们把自己的用例带了进来，而且他们——嗯，他们能摄取数据，他们也构建了那个能力——这是个全新的东西，而且他们起步时，我觉得（这是别人告诉我的，所以可能是道听途说，但我相信）他们甚至在发布之前就已经在和 CTO 们沟通，帮他们理解这一切会走向哪，并获得他们的认可。(00:35:17)：当你说"我们连你的数据都不碰、完全不碰。你就用它来解决问题，然后我们建立信任，再开始集成、接上管道"时，进入企业级就容易得多。但在企业里销售有个挑战，他们会说："好，那我们把你所有数据都接进来……" "哇，那风险极高。"(00:35:41)：所以你得从小处、低风险处起步，比如："嘿，哪一部分客户流失了？我们来想想当时怎么才能让他们更满意，不管怎样。" 所以那部分数据风险较低。所以再说一遍，这也要理解你的市场，理解他们做实验的能力。

turns.en: Oh yes.

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Talk about that.

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: So I personally believe that small business sales is really a, I used to think it was more science than art. Like that early, early, early zero to one. (00:37:33): From one to 10, I think it's more of an art, which is how do I take my learning and how do I package it up where I own the framing, I can speak to very specific alpha, I can vision cast and where I better understand the problem over time better than the market does. And it's all about deal crafting. (00:38:00): They just need to feel like the value they're getting out of it is way more than the cost. And it's sometimes about giving away things that don't really cost much to you, but are super expensive for them. For example, "Hey, we're selling X tool. We can build out Y specifically for you over the next year and integrate it because I know that you would've spent X number of dollars on engineering resources or you wouldn't have gotten in engineering head internally to do this, but we're just leave it to you. You got to give us a year to build it out." (00:38:37): Again, you're not letting them sidetrack you too much, you're kind of containing it. "We'll do that for you at no additional cost." Everyone keeps thinking the product is just what goes into their hand. (00:39:07): The product is pricing. The product is the opportunity, the framing and not letting them compare you to something else. And I know we talked that on our first call, which is as soon as you become a comparison, as soon as you become one of three that they're testing out, you've already sort of lost. It's all about differentiation and it's all about here's what you will be able to do tomorrow because of how we're going to serve you today.
turns.zh: 所以我个人认为，小企业销售其实更偏——我以前觉得它比艺术更像科学。它更多是找出什么行不通、做实验、测试和验证，我确实相信这点，那是为了打基础：我们要在哪个领域玩？我们想做什么？就是那种最早的、最早的从 0 到 1。(00:37:33)：从 1 到 10，我觉得它更像一门艺术，也就是我怎么把学到的东西包装起来，由我来掌控框架，我能讲出非常具体的 alpha，我能描绘愿景，而且随着时间我对问题的理解比市场更深。它全是关于"交易设计"。(00:38:00)：他们只需要感觉自己得到的价值远超成本。这有时候是关于送出那些对你来说成本不高、但对他们来说极其昂贵的东西。比如："嘿，我们在卖 X 工具。我们可以在接下来一年里专门为你构建 Y 并集成进来，因为我知道你本来要花 X 美元在工程资源上，或者你内部根本招不到工程负责人来做这事，但我们直接交给你。你给我们一年时间把它建出来。"(00:38:37)：再说一遍，你没让他们太把你带偏，你某种程度上把它控制住了。"我们免费为你做这件事。" 那是巨大的价值。对吧？或者："嘿，我们要办一场活动，我们希望你站在最前沿。我们希望你当演讲嘉宾。" 巨大的价值。所以就像所有这些额外的、超出产品本身但在价值和愿景上都属于产品一部分的东西。每个人都一直以为产品就是交到他们手里的那个东西。(00:39:07)：产品就是定价。产品就是机会、是对框架的掌控、是不让他们拿你去和别的东西对比。我记得我们第一次通话聊过，就是一旦你变成对比项，一旦你变成他们测试的"三选一"之一，你其实就已经输了。它全是关于差异化，全是关于：因为今天我们会这样服务你，所以明天你将能做到这些。

So you have to decide is this someone you really want to be working with? "Hey, you're spending so much here, why don't we get you to come in and leverage the tool that's been powering this the whole time and move this more into technology serving you versus the human."
