turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So this is a way to make it feel, this is like how you get to 75 to 150K is there's a service attached to it. It's not just, here's my SaaS product, we will solve this problem for you, or a person will be sitting there doing this for you.
turns.zh: 所以这是一种让它感觉自然的方式，也就是你怎么走到 7.5 万到 15 万——是附带了一项服务。不只是"这是我的 SaaS 产品，我们会帮你解决这个问题"，或者"会有一个人坐在那为你做这个"。

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: Or no, it's the technology too. You can add the services. I always, well let me take that back. Whether the services is bundled into it or not, some people will unbundle it, other people will say the services is a part of it. But yeah, it nets out to 75 to 150K. That's right.
turns.zh: 或者不对，技术也是。你可以把服务加进去。我总是——嗯，让我收回那句话。无论服务是否打包进去，有些人会拆开卖，有些人会说服务是其中一部分。但总之，净额是 7.5 万到 15 万。没错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. And you said that it's okay to start lower on ACVs and deals, but you need to push fast towards a 100K over a few months.
turns.zh: 好。你说过从较低的 ACV（平均合同金额）和较小的交易起步是可以的，但你需要在几个月内快速推向 10 万。

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: Yep, that's right. If you can get into an enterprise for 10K in a month, which is not doable, but if you could, and you could go from 10 K to 50 K in four months through an expansion strategy all game, that makes sense, but it's really rare and very hard to do.
turns.zh: 对，没错。如果你能在一个月内以 1 万进一家企业——这不太可能——但如果能，而且你能通过扩张策略在四个月内从 1 万做到 5 万，那说得通，但这真的罕见而且很难做到。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And so there's two different paths there. One is land cheap and grow quickly. The other is move your ACV average up quickly. Seems like both, the latter is probably the more common strategy is just keep increasing prices.
turns.zh: 所以有两条不同的路径。一是低价切入、快速成长。二是快速拉高你的平均 ACV。看起来两者都有，后者可能是更常见的策略——就是不断提价。

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: Yeah, because the former you can get tripped up because they could say, "Okay, now give me an economical price for doing this for a hundred people." And then it all kind of evens out because now you're at the 100K deal anyway, but it's much, there's more room for error, which is why I say go in and try to land 100K.
turns.zh: 对，因为前者你可能会绊倒，因为他们会说："好，现在给我一个做一百人的经济价。" 然后一切差不多拉平，因为你反正也到了 10 万的单，但前者出错的空间大得多，所以我才说进去就尽量拿下 10 万。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: By the way, in our first chat, we talked a lot about the procurement process, which is what trips a lot of people up and is really painful. And I vividly remember that conversation still. So if people are having issues getting through the sales process and procurement, a lot of good advice there.
turns.zh: 顺便说一句，我们第一次聊时，我们聊了很多采购流程，那是让很多人栽跟头、真的很痛苦的东西。我到现在还清楚地记得那次对话。所以如果有人在销售流程和采购上遇到困难，那里有很多好建议。

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: And getting stuck in procurement is usually because you're not speaking to a senior enough person and they don't know how to navigate it, which is why I'm like that executive needs to be involved because as soon as the executive picks up a phone and tries to get a hold of their buying group, things move. (00:48:27): When people say, "Oh, I'm stuck in procurement." I'm like, "Oh, that could just be a qualification error and you never get out of it because you sold to someone too junior." So that's why the 100K is such a safe zone because even for 10K, you might have to go through procurement. So this is the surest way to make sure that you don't ... Listen, I've seen 10K take nine months to close.
turns.zh: 而卡在采购流程里，通常是因为你没在和对足够资深的人聊，他们不知道怎么推进，所以我才说必须有高管参与，因为高管一拿起电话去联系他们的采购小组，事情就动了。(00:48:27)：当人们说"哦，我卡在采购里了"，我会说："哦，那可能只是个筛选错误，你永远出不来，因为你卖给了一个太初级的人。" 所以这就是为什么 10 万是个安全的区间——因为哪怕 1 万的单，你可能也得走采购。所以这是确保你不……听我说，我见过 1 万的单花了九个月才成交。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: No bueno.
turns.zh: 不妙。

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: Yeah, so.
turns.zh: 对，所以。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. Next piece of advice is this idea of vision casting instead of problem solving. So the advice here is instead of here's your problem, here's how our product solves it is here's how you will achieve alpha in the market by adopting the software. We talked about the example of cursor where if you adopt cursor, you're going to draw the 10X engineers that are joining other companies right now. This will give you a big advantage.
turns.zh: 好。下一条建议是"描绘愿景而非解决问题"。所以这里的建议是：与其说"这是你的问题，这是我们的产品怎么解决它"，不如说"采用这个软件，你将在市场上获得怎样的 alpha"。我们聊过 Cursor 的例子：如果你采用 Cursor，你会吸引那些现在正加入其他公司的 10 倍工程师。这会给你巨大优势。

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: That's right. And yeah, it's pain versus opportunity, especially in the age of AI, and I know that we're moving into the next dimension. It's all about solving for a gap. It's seldom about solving for a very, very specific problem because people are trying to figure out what's our AI strategy? Where are we going to go with this? What is the world going to look like? I want to be a part of that new world. So it's a great time to be doing that.
turns.zh: 没错。对，这是"痛点"对"机会"，尤其在 AI 时代，而且我知道我们在进入下一个维度。它全是关于解决"差距"。它很少是关于解决某个非常具体的问题，因为人们正在努力搞清楚：我们的 AI 战略是什么？我们要往哪走？世界会变成什么样？我想成为那个新世界的一部分。所以现在正是做这件事的好时机。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And then there's a bunch of advice you shared about design partners, of just how to select them. Your advice is definitely have design partners because they will help you build the right thing. But as a founder, you need to have a clear vision and sense of where you want to go and not just build everything they're asking you to build.
turns.zh: 然后你还分享了很多关于设计合作伙伴、关于怎么选他们的建议。你的建议是一定要有设计合作伙伴，因为他们会帮你把东西做对。但作为创始人，你得有清晰的愿景和方向感，而不是他们让你建什么你就建什么。

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: That's right, because important to say no. And that's all part of the framing, which is like here's, we want a little skin in the game. You set the price, but here's what we're marching towards in the next six to 12 months. Are we aligned there? If we deliver on what we say we're going to deliver, are we aligned there and do that kind of handshake?
turns.zh: 没错，因为说"不"很重要。而那都是框架的一部分，就像：我们要你也在里面下一点注。你来定价，但这是我们未来 6 到 12 个月要推进的方向。我们在那一点上对齐吗？如果我们兑现了说要交付的东西，我们在那点上对齐吗？然后做个那样的握手约定？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there anything else that I missed that you think is really important for this stage?
turns.zh: 还有什么我漏掉、但你觉得对这个阶段真正重要的吗？

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: So one to 10 is no longer the founder. Maybe the founder comes in very strategic points, but you need a really good enterprise salespeople. Taking someone from small business and expecting them to do enterprise sales, big no-no, it's a different game, right? Vibe like a different game. (00:50:47): You need to understand how corporations buy. You need to understand how executives think. You need to better understand simply just what the enterprise business model is all about and their ability to take on risk. People will bring in super junior enterprise sales reps and I'm like, "You're looking to sell to an executive and you have this person that's five years out of school with no corporate experience doing it, again, unless they have some extremely deep experience in the industry or are just a unicorn in terms of, wow, this person can sell ice to an Eskimo kind of thing." (00:51:27): A junior person converting an executive, again, if the founder is involved, maybe that's doable, but usually the founder can't be involved in every deal and you need people that can, I always say you need people that can cosplay a founder, which is selling the vision, getting them excited, running through a wall to get the deal done and getting creative on ... None of my deals look exactly the same, every deal looks different and that's okay because every organization has slightly different opportunities of where they want to go, and you have to kind of build towards that and the framing may change. (00:52:14): So it's this ability to adapt from what you're hearing and let that compound over time, but I always say, can this person cosplay the founder? I think that that's the best type of salesperson because it doesn't feel like sales. It's more of the art.
turns.zh: 所以从 1 到 10 不再靠创始人了。也许创始人在一些关键节点出现，但你需要真正优秀的企业级销售。把做小企业的人拉来指望他做企业级销售，大忌，这是不同的游戏，对吧？氛围就像不同的游戏。(00:50:47)：你需要理解公司是怎么买的。你需要理解高管怎么想。你需要更清楚地理解企业级商业模式到底是什么、以及他们承担风险的能力。人们会招非常初级的企业级销售代表，而我会说："你想卖给高管，却让一个刚毕业五年、没有任何企业经验的人去做，除非他在行业里有极深的经验，或者就是那种'哇，这人能把冰卖给爱斯基摩人'的奇才。"(00:51:27)：一个初级的人去转化一个高管——再说一遍，如果创始人参与，也许还行，但通常创始人没法参与每一笔交易，而你需要能……的人，我总说你需要能"扮演创始人"的人，也就是卖愿景、让他们兴奋、撞破墙也要把交易做成、并且在……上发挥创意。我的交易没有一笔是完全相同的，每笔都不同，那没问题，因为每个组织想去的方向都略有不同，你得朝那个方向构建，框架也可能变。(00:52:14)：所以它是一种从你听到的东西中适应、并让这种能力随时间复利的能力，但我总说：这个人能"扮演创始人"吗？我觉得那是最好的销售类型，因为它感觉不像销售。它更像一门艺术。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is amazing advice. What is a common profile that you've seen be successful? What level of seniority? What kind of personality and any traits to look for?
turns.zh: 这建议太棒了。你见过成功的人通常是什么画像？什么资历级别？什么性格，以及有什么特质可以留意？

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: Maybe a former founder if you can get that, because they're used to selling, they sold investors and they've sold employees. Two is someone with no sales experience, but has deep product experience or an engineer and can think about things in a unique way where the market is like, "Oh, this is so interesting." (00:53:00): Taking a typical salesperson then and putting them into a sales role almost always is where people get frustrated. The market, it feels salesy. The market doesn't want to be sold to, they want to buy. And I know that it's very hard to hire a really good enterprise salesperson. The number of people that I've interviewed, I can count on my hand the ones that I get really, really excited by. (00:53:29): It's almost like coming across a great founder. It's not as common as everyone expects, and I think that that's true for engineering. I think that that's true for sales and I think a lot of people, sales is like, "Oh, just throw a body into it. The product will do the work."
turns.zh: 如果能找到，也许是前创始人，因为他们习惯销售，他们卖过投资人、也卖过员工。第二是没有任何销售经验、但有深厚产品经验或是个工程师、能用独特方式思考、让市场觉得"哦，这真有意思"的人。(00:53:00)：把典型的销售员拉来放进销售角色，几乎总是让人受挫的地方。市场会觉得"很销售腔"。市场不想要被推销，他们想要买。而且我知道招一个真正好的企业级销售非常难。我面试过那么多人，能让我真正、真正兴奋的，用手指头数得过来。(00:53:29)：这几乎就像遇到一位优秀的创始人。它没大家以为的那么常见，而且我觉得工程也是这样。我觉得销售也是这样，而很多人觉得销售就是："哦，随便塞个人进去。产品会搞定一切的。"

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Advice I often hear is don't hire a senior VP of salesperson from a bigger company. Do you agree with that? What's like to senior?
turns.zh: 我经常听到的建议是：别从大公司挖一个资深销售VP。你同意吗？什么叫"太资深"？

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: Yeah, so the bigger company thing, the brand was doing all of the work. The brand built the trust. You need this person to be able to build the trust and they're usually, the product is still so new. The product is the founder in the zero to one stage. The product is just starting to get a case study. (00:54:15): You probably have maybe a few references, but it's still very, very early days. You need the market to believe the salesperson and you need that market to know that they're trustworthy. A VP of sales at a large company, I would say, they're best suited for a large company because one to 10, you're running through walls. (00:54:33): You have to figure out, you're doing a lot of convincing, you're doing a lot of educating, you're doing a lot of creative deal crafting. A lot of owning the frame. It's not necessarily selling a product, it's selling that future value, which a VP of sales at a large companies, it's very different. It's a different game. It's kind of like the SMB and enterprise.
turns.zh: 对，关于大公司那点——品牌在做所有的工作。品牌建立了信任。你需要这个人能去建立信任，而通常，产品还那么新。在从 0 到 1 阶段，产品就是创始人。产品才刚开始有案例。(00:54:15)：你大概只有几个参考客户，但还非常非常早期。你需要市场相信这个销售，你需要市场知道他们可信。大公司的销售 VP，我会说最适合大公司，因为从 1 到 10，你是在撞墙。(00:54:33)：你得想办法，你要做大量说服、大量教育、大量创造性的交易设计。大量掌控框架。它不一定是卖产品，是卖那个未来价值，而大公司的销售 VP，那是很不一样的。是不同的游戏。有点像 SMB 和企业级的区别。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's interesting you said when you described the profile of a great hire here is you said they don't need to have done sales. If they have done sales, what's a number years or kind of what do you look for that tells you, "Okay, this is a good fit for the first hire."
turns.zh: 有意思的是，你描述优秀 hire 的画像时，说他们不需要做过销售。如果他们做过销售，多少年经验、或者你看重什么信号能告诉你"好，这适合作为第一个 hire"？

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: I actually think it's less about experience and more about the person. Does this person make you feel good? Do you want to buy from this person? I think Jason, Jason Lemkin said that best. Would you want to buy from this person?
turns.zh: 其实我觉得经验没那么重要，更重要的是这个人。这个人让你感觉舒服吗？你愿意从这个人手里买东西吗？我觉得 Jason，Jason Lemkin 说得最好：你会愿意从这个人手里买吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Can they sell you a pen?
turns.zh: 他们能把一支笔卖给你吗？

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: The classic. Yeah, exactly. Do they mimic or mirror the market they're selling to? It's much easier to buy from someone that looks and feels like you than it does from somebody that's in a totally different realm. And also, an executive wants to talk to another senior person. (00:55:41): They don't want to talk to someone that just graduated from college and is selling them the new way of working. What do they know? So I think it's tricky. I would say someone with no sales experience makes it feel different and special, that's what I like about it. Someone with sales experience knows how to navigate and probably be qualified better, but it's almost like the blend of those two things. (00:56:05): And that's why I go back to cosplaying the founder, which is like, could this person close a future employee? Do they get excited about the problems they're solving internally and the vision that they get to sell to?
turns.zh: 经典。对，没错。他们会不会模仿、映照他们要卖的对象所在的市场？从一个和你长相、感觉都像的人手里买，比从一个完全不同的领域的人手里买要容易得多。而且，高管想和另一个资深的人聊。(00:55:41)：他们不想和一个刚毕业、在向他们推销新工作方式的人聊。他们懂什么？所以我觉得这很微妙。我会说，没有销售经验的人会让它感觉不同、特别，这是我喜欢的地方。有销售经验的人知道怎么推进、可能更会做资格筛选，但它几乎像是这两者的结合。(00:56:05)：所以我才回到"扮演创始人"——这个人能搞定一个未来的员工吗？他们对自己在内部解决的问题、以及要卖出去的愿景感到兴奋吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This actually was a reader question, listener question from Twitter. So Peter Dedenne asked, "How do you make this first salesperson as enthusiastic about the product as you? Is there something you could do? Is it more just they already are and you just leverage that?"
turns.zh: 这其实是个读者问题，来自 Twitter 的听众提问。Peter Dedenne 问："你怎么让第一个销售对你的产品和你一样充满热情？有没有你能做的事？还是说他们本来就热情，你只是加以利用？"

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: Incentives. Salespeople love to make money.
turns.zh: 激励。销售员最爱赚钱。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Easy.
turns.zh: 简单。

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: So if they know it's possible, if they know it's possible, you'll be shocked what people can get done.
turns.zh: 所以如果他们知道这是可能的——如果他们知道这是可能的——你会惊讶人们能做成什么。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: If they see how much they could make. Amazing. I imagine there still also has to be an innate excitement about the product and the opportunity.
turns.zh: 如果他们看到自己能赚多少。太棒了。我猜想，对产品和机会本身还是得有一种天生的兴奋感。

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: They have to believe in it. They have to believe in the founder, but incentives usually make the world go round, but yeah, is this person, are they asking the right questions to the founder? The best thing to do is have the founder join the first five calls. You know after five calls if this person has what it takes, and don't be afraid to fire. One in every two salespeople usually are fired. Yeah, it's a very high failure rate.
turns.zh: 他们必须相信它。他们必须相信创始人，但激励通常让世界运转，不过对，这个人会不会向创始人问对的问题？最好的做法是让创始人参加前五次通话。五次通话后你就知道这个人行不行，而且别怕开除。每两个销售里通常就有一个被开除。对，失败率非常高。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Because you can tell pretty quickly how it's going.
turns.zh: 因为你很快就能看出进展如何。

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: You can tell, or the vision of the founders is just very wrong.
turns.zh: 你能看出，或者创始人的愿景本身就是错的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Speaking of incentives, do you have any quick advice on how to structure their comp? Just like how much they earn?
turns.zh: 说到激励，关于怎么设计他们的薪酬结构，你有什么快速建议吗？比如他们能赚多少？

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: It's usually 50/50. So it's 50% OTE. So it's 50% base salary, 50% OTE.
turns.zh: 通常是 50/50。也就是 50% 的 OTE（目标总薪酬）。所以是 50% 底薪，50% OTE。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And then how much of the sale do they typically get? Say the first sales hire.
turns.zh: 那他们通常能拿到销售额的多少？比如第一个销售 hire。

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: It depends on the size of the deal, but in technology, it could be anywhere between eight and 12%. So rounds out around 10%.
turns.zh: 看交易大小，但在科技行业，可能在 8% 到 12% 之间。所以大概在 10% 左右。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. Awesome. When do you hire the first salesperson? Is it around the 1 million ARR mark usually?
turns.zh: 好。太好了。你什么时候招第一个销售？通常是在 100 万 ARR 这个节点吗？

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: Yeah, it's around that 1 million ARR, mark and I, and it's usually when you have your first seven to 10 customers and there's some pattern recognition around it that you can share with somebody else, there's some consistencies. Otherwise, it's just like that would be very hard.
turns.zh: 对，大约在 100 万 ARR 这个节点，而且通常是当你有了头 7 到 10 个客户，并且围绕它有了一些可以被识别的规律、可以分享给别人，有了一些一致性。否则，那会非常难。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Basically as a founder, you have to figure out how to sell enough times so that you can show someone, "Here's what's working."
turns.zh: 基本上作为创始人，你得想清楚怎么把东西卖足够多次，这样你才能向别人展示："这是行得通的。"

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: And this is the common thing I hear, "Well, I'm a $10 million business. I'm in this small business space. You're $0 in enterprise." It's a zero to one right now in enterprise. It's a totally different game. It's a different value proposition, it's a different deal structuring, it's a different target market. It's a different risk tolerance. It's totally different. So don't be blindsided when-
turns.zh: 而我常听到这种话："嗯，我是家 1000 万美元的公司。我在小企业这个领域。你在企业级还是 0。" 现在在企业级就是从 0 到 1。是完全不同的游戏。不同的价值主张，不同的交易结构，不同的目标市场。不同的风险承受度。完全不同。所以当你……时不要被打了个措手不及——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It doesn't work.
turns.zh: 它行不通。

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: ... There's a lot of unlearning that needs to happen when you move into a new market.
turns.zh: ……当你进入一个新市场时，有很多东西需要"忘掉重学"。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So the advice here is make yourself sell up until around a million ARR, especially if you're trying to go enterprise selling to enterprises yourself as a founder, which is really hard. You have so much to do and you have to be selling this thing for a long time time.
turns.zh: 所以这里的建议是：让自己一直卖到大约 100 万 ARR，尤其是如果你作为创始人想自己去跑企业级销售，那真的很难。你有太多事要做，而且你得把这个东西卖很长一段时间。

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: Yep. And then try and find someone that you get excited by. It's funny, if you ask the founder, are you excited by your salesperson? I'm curious what the real answer is. It's like, "Well, it's a button to see it in. It was hard to hire, so."
turns.zh: 对。然后试着去找一个让你兴奋的人。有意思的是，如果你问创始人"你对你的销售兴奋吗？"我好奇真实的答案是什么。大概会是："嗯，能看到他就不错了。招聘太难了，所以。"

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Interesting. I remember, I think it was Jason's advice was to hire two people immediately.
turns.zh: 有意思。我记得，我想那是 Jason 的建议——立刻招两个人。

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: That's right.
turns.zh: 没错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So you can compare them. Do you agree with that?
turns.zh: 这样你就能对比他们。你同意吗？

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: 100%. Yeah, because of the 50% failure rate. I think that's exactly right. So yeah, even a tall order, go find two people that are good. But yeah, I think that that's right because one in two will fail.
turns.zh: 百分之百。对，因为 50% 的失败率。我觉得完全正确。所以哪怕很难，也去找两个靠谱的人。但确实，我觉得没错，因为每两个就有一个会失败。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, let me ask you another reader question from Hang Huang. This is kind of in a different direction. So he says, "The biggest challenge is always cutting through the noise to get that initial meeting with the right decision maker. How do you even get their attention?"
turns.zh: 好，让我再问一个来自 Hang Huang 的读者问题。这个方向有点不同。他说："最大的挑战永远是如何穿透噪音，争取到和正确决策者初次见面的机会。你到底怎么引起他们的注意？"

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: It's the vision. What is the opportunity that you're selling? That if they are excited by that, they will take a call. I see it all the time, and don't give away the farm. Keep it to three sentences. And I know I said this on our first call, but say something counterintuitive, they could feel different. Make it feel like they can learn from you by taking a 15-minute call. You see the standards of like, "Oh, I came across your LinkedIn." And, "Are you looking to grow your business by 15%?" It's like, "What kind of statement is that?"
turns.zh: 靠愿景。你卖的是什么机会？如果他们对此兴奋，他们会接电话。我天天看到这种情况，而且别"把整个农场都送出去"。控制在三句话。我在第一次通话也说过，但要说点反直觉的东西，让他们感觉不一样。让他们觉得花 15 分钟通个电话能从你身上学到东西。你看那些套路，比如"哦，我偶然看到你的 LinkedIn"，还有"你想让业务增长 15% 吗？" 就像"这算什么话？"

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And this is in the cold email they get about this pitch.
turns.zh: 而这出现在他们收到的这条冷邮件的 pitch 里。

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. So this is a good segue to another reader question from Hugo Alves, Co-Founder of Synthetic users. He asked, "What's the best advice for going from healthy inbound to targeted outbound?"
turns.zh: 太棒了。所以这是个很好的过渡，引向另一个来自 Hugo Alves（Synthetic Users 联合创始人）的读者问题。他问："从健康的自然引流（inbound）转向有目标的主动出击（outbound），最好的建议是什么？"

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: Healthy inbound usually is a marketing-led initiative. So that's a marketing game. It depends what deal value you're selling. Are you selling a $5,000 deal? It's got to be marketing-led to make the engine work. If you're selling $100,000 deal, you're doing outbound day one. So again, it breaks it into those. This is like that blending of the, I see a blending of that question. This is where you're doing small business marketing-led activities or are you a sales-led organization selling a $100,000 deal?
turns.zh: 健康 inbound 通常是个营销驱动的动作。所以那是营销的游戏。这取决于你卖的交易价值。你是卖 5000 美元的单？那必须靠营销驱动才能让引擎运转。如果你卖 10 万美元的单，你从第一天起就在做 outbound。所以又回到了那两套划分。这就像那个问题的混合——我看到这个问题的混合点。你是做小企业营销驱动的活动，还是一家销售驱动、卖 10 万美元单的组织？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And the reason that's important, just in case it's not obvious, is you're not going to make money if you're selling. People are spending time closing deals that are making 10, 20K. Just the ROI on that won't work for your business model.
turns.zh: 而这一点重要的原因——以防不明显——是如果你在卖……你是赚不到钱的。人们花时间去关那些只赚 1 万、2 万的单。光是那个 ROI 就对你的商业模式行不通。

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: That's right. Yep.
turns.zh: 对。没错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. By the way, let me just say, Jen, this is an incredible conversation already. We've gone-
turns.zh: 太棒了。顺便说一句，Jen，我想说，这已经是一场非常精彩的对话了。我们已经——

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: Oh this awesome.
turns.zh: 哦，太棒了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: ... Through so much. This is exactly what I was hoping to get through and we've gone through so much advice that I think is going to be so helpful to so many people. There's a few things that your partner, Justin also suggested I ask you about that I want to touch on. One is you have this question you ask founders a lot that opens up their mind. You ask them, "If you give your product away for free, would people even use this?" And every founder is like, "Of course." And then you ask, "A customer this?" And they're like, "Nah, we wouldn't use this." And that just blows their mind. Talk about just the power of that and how you recommend people approach this.
turns.zh: 聊了这么多。这正是我希望覆盖的，而且我们过了这么多建议，我觉得对很多人会非常有帮助。还有几件事是你的搭档 Justin 建议我问你的，我想提一下。其中一件是你经常问创始人、能打开他们思路的一个问题。你问他们："如果你把产品免费送出去，会有人用吗？" 每个创始人都会说："当然。" 然后你问："客户会（用）这个吗？" 他们就会说："不会，我们不会用这个。" 那直接把他们震住了。聊聊这个的威力，以及你建议人们怎么运用它。

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: I always say ask the questions you're afraid to because that truth is going to get you closer and closer to the answer. So I'll ask a client straight up on a call, I'll say, "Honestly, do we think we're going to get the deal done this year? Is it possible?" They'll give you the real answer and people are afraid to ask. But the other side is sort of if they're in it with you, they don't care about that question, right? (01:03:01): Can't ask that question on day one, but if you are, and we didn't talk about this, but maybe this is important. Every single enterprise deal I have done, the deal is done, the deal is closed and pretty much done through text. It's not on email anymore. It is a relationship you're building with someone where if my enterprise client called me, I'm picking up that phone immediately or I'm responding them to immediately because that builds so much trust. (01:03:31): If they know they can call on you, they're going to get you to pick up and they know that you're going to do everything humanly possible to make sure that this is successful. People will turn over rocks for you. I have a client at a Fortune 10 company where I was like, it's so important we get the deal done this year. Is that possible? And she's like, it's a tall order, but if it's going to help you, let's do it. (01:04:00): These are how enterprise deals gets done, it's relationships and it's this, and this is why I'm saying structuring the deal, make it feel like you went to bat for them and in often cases, you are going to bat for them and structure it in a way that makes sense for them. Everyone kind of just tries and pigeonhole. Pigeonholing and deal structuring consistency is important for a $10,000, sub-$10,000 deal. A $100,000 deal, it very commonly will look different every time.
turns.zh: 我总说，去问那些你不敢问的问题，因为那个真相会让你离答案越来越近。所以我会在通话里直接问客户："老实说，你觉得我们今年能把这笔交易做成吗？可能吗？" 他们会给你真实的答案，而人们不敢问。但另一方面，如果他们和你是一条船上的，他们不在乎这个问题，对吧？(01:03:01)：第一天不能问那个问题，但如果你问了——我们没聊过这个，但也许这很重要。我做的每一笔企业级交易，都是成交的、关掉的，而且几乎都是通过文字（即时消息）完成的。不再是邮件了。你是在和某个人建立一段关系——如果我的企业客户给我打电话，我会立刻接起，或者立刻回复，因为那建立了极大的信任。(01:03:31)：如果他们知道可以找你，他们会让你接起，而且他们知道你会尽一切人力所及确保这事成功。人们会为你全力以赴去铺路。我在一家财富 10 强企业有位客户，当时我说，今年把这笔交易做成非常重要。可能吗？她说，这是个很高的要求，但如果能帮到你，那我们就做。(01:04:00)：企业级交易就是这样达成的，靠关系，靠这个，所以我才说要设计好交易，让它感觉像是你为他们出头力争，而且很多时候你确实在为他们出头，并以对他们有意义的方式去设计它。大家多少都在试图把它套进固定框里。把交易套进固定框、保持结构一致，对 1 万美元、1 万以下的小单很重要。而 10 万美元的单，通常每次看起来都不一样。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: April Dunford was on the podcast and she shared this really interesting insight that the reason people behave this way is the person at the company buying this thing, their ass is on the line Also, their reputation is on the line for this thing to work out. So they want it to go really well.
turns.zh: April Dunford 上过这个播客，她分享了一个很有意思的洞察：人们之所以这样表现，是因为公司里买这东西的人，他们的"屁股"是在线上的——也就是说，这事能不能成，他们的声誉也绑在上面。所以他们希望它真的顺利。

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: That's right. Again, they do this one in every three years, one in every two years, maybe one in every five years. Hell, I don't know. They don't do this every year. It's very rare. It's no one likes a new tool. No one. Not you, not me, unless it changes everything.
turns.zh: 没错。再说一遍，他们每三年做一次、每两年做一次，也许每五年做一次。鬼知道。他们不是每年都做。非常罕见。没人喜欢新工具。没人。不是你，不是我，除非它能改变一切。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. Figma was a great example, that's Slack.
turns.zh: 对。Figma 是个好例子，Slack 也是。

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: Everything you've touched
turns.zh: 你接触过的每一样东西

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Everything that worked out. You said that you asked these questions that people are afraid to ask. What are some other examples of questions you often ask that people are afraid to ask?
turns.zh: 所有成功的东西。你说你会问那些人们不敢问的问题。还有什么你常问、而人们不敢问的问题的例子？

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: I will say, "Listen, this is $150,000 engagement. I will co-author it with you where we can make this a little bit bigger if you need something else. We can make it a little bit smaller in year one, but in year two it steps up. How do we get this done so when you go to bat, it's a win?" Sell them, do they take it to the wrong side and try and discount you? I've actually never seen that because at that point you have a relationship. (01:05:51): So co-authoring the pricing is so important because they need to know that they go to bat, they can say, "I got this out of them. If we get this deal done." So this is why when I say every deal looks the same, you're asking great questions because it's explaining why I meant by that, but this is another example of why every deal in the enterprise sort of looks somewhat different because a lot of it is co-authored. So again, if someone wants a slightly lower price, give it to them, but maybe them lock them in a little bit longer.
turns.zh: 我会说："听我说，这是一个 15 万美元的合作。我会和你共同拟定它——如果你需要别的，我们可以让它稍微大一点。第一年我们可以让它小一点，但第二年会上调。我们怎么把它做成，让你去力争时能是个赢？" 卖给他们时，他们会把它带到错误的一方、试图给你打折吗？我还真没见过，因为到那个点上你们已经有了关系。(01:05:51)：所以共同拟定定价非常重要，因为他们需要知道，当他们去力争时，他们能说："我从他们那争取到了这个。如果我们做成这笔交易。" 所以这就是为什么我说每笔交易看起来都一样——你问的好问题其实是在解释我那句话的意思——但这也是为什么企业里的每笔交易看起来都有点不同的另一个例子，因为很多是共同拟定的。所以再说一遍，如果有人想要略低一点的价格，给他们，但也许把他们的合约锁得长一点。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's another point that Justin makes that you've touched on a bit, but it's when your no, the way he phrased it is, Jen always talks about how no is the best answer to yes because no is data that you can use. Talk about that.
turns.zh: Justin 还提了一点，你稍微提过，就是当你的回答是"不"——他原话是：Jen 总说"不"是对"是"最好的回答，因为"不"是你能用的数据。聊聊这个。

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: I am a qualification crazy person. I will not get in on another call with someone because on the first call it's either a yes or a no, there's no in between. Humans are, we're so different and we're so unpredictable, but we're also so predictable at the same time, right? It's very obvious if someone is excited and wants to do something, it is so obvious when someone is just trying to be nice. (01:07:06): So I will say to them on that call, "I'm sort of getting the vibe that this might not be a good fit or might not be good timing. Did I misinterpret that?" And they will usually say, "Yeah, you're right, it's probably not a good fit." And then immediately, "Great, I would love to stay in touch. You've just saved a relationship and you've just saved yourself a ton of time."
turns.zh: 我是个"资格筛选疯子"。我不会再和某个人约第二次通话，因为第一次通话要么是"是"要么是"不"，没有中间地带。人是——我们如此不同、如此不可预测，但同时我们又如此可预测，对吧？如果一个人兴奋、想做这件事，那非常明显；当一个人只是出于礼貌，那也如此明显。(01:07:06)：所以我会在那次通话里对他们说："我有点感觉这可能不太合适，或者时机不对。是我理解错了吗？" 而他们通常会说："对，你说得对，可能不太合适。" 然后我立刻说："好，我很乐意保持联系。你刚刚挽救了一段关系，也省了自己一大堆时间。"

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And the implication here is just to your point, you're limited on time. You don't want to be spending time going down or rival that won't you anywhere.
turns.zh: 而这里的意思是，正如你说的，你的时间有限。你不想把时间花在一条不会带你去任何地方的死胡同或竞争上。

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: Yeah, exactly.
turns.zh: 对，没错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm going to take a quick tangent on tools. What's the state of the art on go-to-market outbound tooling?
turns.zh: 我想稍微岔开一下，聊工具。目前在 GTM（进入市场）outbound 工具方面，最前沿的是什么？

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: I don't use a tool because I believe in the manual and I'll explain why. Every single note I send is slightly different because I see a picture of them and I'm like, "Oh, I don't know if that's going to land." Or I'm like, "Oh, they actually might appreciate this. It's weird." Visual cues are so helpful. A picture is a visual cue, looking at how long they've been in the role, looking how long they've been at the company. (01:08:05): I use all of these little things and I seldom customize a note in a way that people expect which is that first customized sentence because AI does that, and everyone's doing that. So I go the opposite extreme, which is like remove it and I customize it with how I frame it or the subject line. So it's like if I'm talking to someone like a peer, I might say quick question like QQ. (01:08:36): If I'm talking to someone that has a bit more experience, I might write a little bit of a tighter note, not all lowercase. So it just depends on who you're speaking to. And again, this is why it's okay to spend a little bit of time on this because it's a hundred thousand dollars. It's actually a million dollars at the end of the day because a $100,000 deal if you play your cards right turns into a million dollar deal over three to five years.
turns.zh: 我不用工具，因为我相信"手动"，我来解释为什么。我发的每一条信息都略有不同，因为我看到他们的照片就会想："哦，我不知道那个会不会奏效。" 或者："哦，他们可能反而欣赏这个。挺怪的。" 视觉线索非常有用。照片是个视觉线索，看他们在这个职位上待了多久、在这家公司待了多久。(01:08:05)：我用上所有这些小细节，而且我很少用人们预期的那种方式去定制——就是第一句定制的客套话，因为 AI 会那么做，大家都在那么做。所以我走相反的极端，也就是把它去掉，然后用我怎么定框架、或者主题行来定制。比如如果我和一个人像同辈那样聊，我可能会说"quick question"之类的 QQ。(01:08:36)：如果我和更有经验的人聊，我可能会写一个更紧凑的便条，不全小写。所以这取决于你在和谁聊。再说一遍，这就是为什么花一点时间在这上面是可以的，因为它值 10 万美元。说到底它其实是 100 万美元，因为一笔 10 万美元的交易如果打得好，三到五年内会变成 100 万美元的交易。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love how much you enjoy this. It's so fun to, so essentially what are you doing? You're sitting on LinkedIn finding folks to ping and then you cold email them one individually, manually.
turns.zh: 我好喜欢你多享受这件事。这太有意思了，所以你本质上在做什么？你坐在 LinkedIn 上找人去联系，然后一个一个手动给他们发冷邮件。

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: It's so weird, Lenny, I have no process. I kind of just go with the vibe. I'll read an article about Tesla and I'm like, "Huh, they could be interested in this." Not because that article had anything to do with the problem I'm solving, but because I'm like, "This feels like a good Tesla day." It's hard to describe. It's a very emotional thing for me, and not to toot my own horn, obviously, but I've been successful in sales and the most successful sales people can't explain why they're good at it. (01:09:51): It just comes to them naturally. It's just like an emotional thing. It's like the world's best founders. How do you be a good founder? It's very, very hard to define. How do you become a good engineer? Very, very hard to define. So I don't believe in playbooks. I believe that there's a feel to it. I emailed a chief legal officer at a hedge fund once and he responded to me because I wrote to him on Saturday. I knew it was going to be busy. I made it one sentence and it was tweaked for him.
turns.zh: 这很怪，Lenny，我没有任何流程。我基本就是跟着感觉走。我会读一篇关于特斯拉的文章，然后想："嗯，他们可能对这个感兴趣。" 不是因为那篇文章和我解决的问题有什么关系，而是因为我觉得"今天是个适合联系特斯拉的好日子"。很难形容。这对我来说是非常情绪化的事，而且显然不是自吹自擂，但我在销售上成功了，而最成功的销售员也说不清自己为什么擅长。(01:09:51)：它就是自然地来到他们身上。就是一种情绪化的东西。就像世界上最优秀的创始人。怎么做一个好创始人？非常非常难定义。怎么成为一个好工程师？非常非常难定义。所以我不相信"剧本"。我相信这里面有一种"手感"。我有一次给一家对冲基金的首席法务官发邮件，他回复了我，因为我是在周六给他写的。我知道那天会很忙。我把它写成一句话，而且是专门为他调过的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Do you feel like this is going to be the way as AI SDRs just kind of take over and everyone's getting billions of emails that feel AI-ish?
turns.zh: 你觉得随着 AI SDR（销售开发代表）接管、每个人都收到几十亿封感觉"很 AI"的邮件，这种方式还会是主流吗？

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 会。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So I guess maybe speak more there. Just like is the alpha essentially just become human? Don't automate? Should you think you should?
turns.zh: 那也许再多说一点。是不是说，alpha 本质上就是"变得人性化"？不要自动化？你怎么看？

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: The thing about AI tools is they're all pulling from the same databases. So I'm like, "I want to email someone not in the database that's getting hit by a million folks. I want to take a back door in, not the front door where everyone else is trick-or-treating."
turns.zh: AI 工具的问题在于，它们都从同样的数据库里抓取数据。所以我会想："我想发邮件给那些不在数据库里、没被千万人轰炸过的人。我想走后门进去，而不是走所有人都去'不给糖就捣蛋'的前门。"

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And this is effective for very large deal, which is what you need to be doing anyway because it takes a lot of time to do it this way.
turns.zh: 而这招对非常大的交易有效——反正你本来就该做这种大交易，因为这样做很花时间。

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Interesting. So you're not like sitting in Clay, you're not like Apollo, I don't have all those tools. You're just finding people yourself.
turns.zh: 有意思。所以你不是坐在 Clay 里，不是用 Apollo，我可没有那些工具。你只是自己在找人。

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: Yep.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Do you start with a target prospect list at least just like, "Here's the companies that are the perfect fit for this and let's work through them."
turns.zh: 你至少会从一个目标客户清单开始吧，比如"这些就是完美契合的公司，我们一个个过"？

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: It's all in my brain. I've been doing this for so long, I have in my brain, I'm like, these are my early adopters. These who I'm going to go to after I close those logos, they get excited by those logos. So it's just experience of you land a Walmart, you're going to go to the rest of the industry and say, "Hey, we're working with Walmart." Versus you go to some lower end enterprise company and they're like, "Wait, what do you do?" I can't even comprehend. (01:12:02): Also, the most strategic people, some of the most strategic executives are at these tier one logos. That's why they're tier one because they've got super smart, really capable folks. They also extract the best talent, the best talent likes to experiment and continue to improve. So it's like this compounding thing.
turns.zh: 全在我脑子里。我做这行太久了，我在脑子里有：这些是我的早期采用者。这些是我拿下那些 logo 之后要去找的人，他们会被那些 logo 激发兴趣。所以这就是经验：你拿下了沃尔玛，你就会去行业里其他人那里说："嘿，我们在和沃尔玛合作。" 而如果你去某个低端企业级公司，他们会说："等等，你们是做什么的？" 我完全无法理解。(01:12:02)：而且，最有战略眼光的人、一些最有战略眼光的高管都在这些一线 logo 里。这就是为什么它们是一线，因为他们有超级聪明、非常能干的人。他们也能吸引最优秀的人才，而最优秀的人才喜欢做实验、持续进步。所以这就像一种复利。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: For someone that isn't Jen and has all this experience, say their founder, they're hit a million ARR. They're just like, "Okay, where do we find our customers?" Do you have any advice for just coming up with who we should go after? Should they be using these tools? Should they be hiring someone like a Jen? I know this is what you do for companies. So one crowd is go hire JJELLYFISH to help them through this.
turns.zh: 对于一个不是 Jen、没有这么多经验的人，比如一位创始人，他们做到了 100 万 ARR。他们就会想："好，我们去哪找客户？" 关于怎么想清楚该追谁，你有什么建议？他们应该用这些工具吗？他们应该雇一个像 Jen 这样的人吗？我知道你对公司做的就是这事。所以一个方向是去雇 JJELLYFISH 来帮他们度过这个阶段。

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: Founder, the founder. I would say the founder, this is sort of in tune with them in a way. They just have to find it. It's so weird to say it's all, and I hate saying it because it's like a commonplace thing to say, but it's like there's this thing about flow and it's like some of these brands are in flow with you right now, right? You found this insight from somewhere. Who else? What's the next adjacent ring of people that would buy into that?
turns.zh: 创始人，是创始人。我会说创始人，在某种意义上是和这些（客户）同频的。他们只是得找到它。说"全都在……"很奇怪，而且我讨厌这么说，因为这像句陈词滥调，但确实有种"心流"的东西，就是当下有些品牌正和你在同一个频率上，对吧？你从某处发现了这个洞察。还有谁？下一个相邻的、会认同这个的人群圈层是哪些？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And so what I'm hearing is just pay attention to what's happening, what companies are-
turns.zh: 所以我听到的是：只要留意正在发生的事、哪些公司正在——

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The news, what companies are doing interesting things, who are the kind of early adopters in the market.
turns.zh: 新闻，哪些公司在做有意思的事，市场里的早期采用者都是谁。

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: If it was just a database list and it was just about figuring out the right messaging and then emailing folks, we would've known by that by now.
turns.zh: 如果只靠一个数据库清单、只靠想出对的文案然后发邮件给人，那我们早该知道（怎么做了）。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's so interesting. Okay, maybe one more question. This again is from Justin. He shares that when you hit resistance, you never argue, you reframe. If someone says, "We already have X solution, you'll agree and pivot and totally X is great for this thing, but here's what we can do."
turns.zh: 那太有意思了。好，也许再来一个问题。这又来自 Justin。他分享说，当你遇到阻力时，你从不争辩，而是重新框定（reframe）。如果有人说："我们已经有 X 解决方案了"，你会表示同意并转向，完全承认 X 在这件事上很棒，但接着说我们能做的事。

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: This is why it's sell to the alpha. Hey, I know. Listen, that problem you just described, you're right. You have a tool for that. We're taking you much further upstream with value. This is the opportunity I want you guys to have access to.
turns.zh: 这就是为什么是"卖 alpha"。嘿，我知道。听我说，你刚才描述的问题，你说得对。你有个工具解决那个。我们是带你去价值更上游的地方。这是我希望你们能用上的机会。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love it, Jen. I've gone through everything I was hoping to get through. On the other hand, I feel like we could do another hour on all these things, I feel like we need to do.
turns.zh: 太喜欢了，Jen。我已经把我们想覆盖的都覆盖了。话说回来，我觉得这些事我们还能再聊一个小时，我觉得我们还需要聊。

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: We have three.
turns.zh: 我们有第三期了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, we need round three on the next phase and all the things that people want to dig further into. Before we get to our very exciting lightning round, is there anything else that you wanted to touch on or share?
turns.zh: 对，我们需要第三期，讲下一阶段，以及大家想深入挖掘的所有东西。在我们进入非常精彩的快问快答之前，还有什么你想提或想分享的吗？

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: This stuff is really hard. It's very hard. Sales is also all about learning very, very quickly from the rejection. The rejection is good because it's a forced learning and you never want to go through that again, but you have to be, I don't like to use the word cringe. You can't be afraid to cringe is like bringing your AI recorder into a call, that's cringey, but sending 15 notes to people that you can deliver serious value to, don't be afraid, and don't be afraid to ask the hard questions. Be different. (01:15:12): The whole game is about, "Oh, this feels different. That's what people want access to." Yet everyone commoditizes themselves. They try and mimic what everyone, they try and mimic a forward deployed engineer. Just rename it. You don't have to use the same nomenclature. Everyone gets excited by the new because the new could be the next thing, the thing that changes it all. So that's why I'm always like, "Don't be better. Be different."
turns.zh: 这事儿真的很难。非常难。销售也全是关于从拒绝中非常非常快地学习。拒绝是好事，因为它是被迫的学习，你再也不想经历那种事，但你必须……我不喜欢用"社死（cringe）"这个词。你不能害怕"社死"——比如把你的 AI 录音器带进通话，那挺社死的，但给那些你能提供真正价值的人发 15 条信息，别害怕，也别害怕问那些难的问题。要不一样。(01:15:12)：整个游戏在于"哦，这感觉不一样。那就是人们想要接触的东西。" 然而每个人都把自己商品化了。他们试图模仿所有人，他们试图模仿一个"前沿部署工程师"。改个名就行。你不必用同样的术语。每个人都会为"新"而兴奋，因为新可能就是下一个东西、那个改变一切的东西。所以我总说："不要做得更好。要做得不同。"

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: An amazing way to end it. With that, Jen, we've reached our very exciting lightning round. I've got five questions for you. Are you ready?
turns.zh: 完美的收尾方式。那么，Jen，我们进入了非常精彩的快问快答环节。我有五个问题给你。准备好了吗？

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 好了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: First question, what are two or three books that you find yourself recommending most to other people?
turns.zh: 第一个问题，有哪两三本书是你最常推荐给别人的？

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: I do Twitter accounts.
turns.zh: 我推的是 Twitter 账号。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh, Twitter accounts to follow? Oh, amazing.
turns.zh: 哦，是值得关注的 Twitter 账号？哦，太棒了。

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay.
turns.zh: 好。

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: Lenny, the day I have time to read a book.
turns.zh: Lenny，等到我有时间读书的那天吧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Period.
turns.zh: 就这样。

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: Period. I would love to be reading books.
turns.zh: 就这样。我很想读书。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Cool. Twitter accounts to follow. Tell me.
turns.zh: 酷。值得关注的 Twitter 账号。说说看。

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: Yeah. Look, obviously you, you produce some of the best content, truthfully,
turns.zh: 对。看，显然是你，你生产了一些最好的内容，说真的，

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Appreciate it.
turns.zh: 谢谢。

turns.en: You get into the minds of people that they're not even giving this insight on Twitter. Who else do I absolutely love? Jason Lemkin. So for sales, Jason Lemkin is awesome, awesome follow for sales, and also he had a great, great recording with you. So link to that because that was a great piece. I actually learned a ton from Matt. I love Gavin Baker. Super nuanced takes. Takes a lot of obvious statements, but shares a lot of the non-obvious insight. He's great. Jason Cohen, have you ever had Jason Cohen on the cast?
turns.zh: 你能深入那些人在 Twitter 上都不会分享的洞察。还有谁我绝对喜欢？Jason Lemkin。所以在销售上，Jason Lemkin 超棒，关注他做销售超赞，而且他和你也做过一期很棒的录音。放个链接吧，因为那期很精彩。我其实从 Matt 那学了很多。我喜欢 Gavin Baker。非常细腻的见解。他会接很多显而易见的陈述，却分享很多不显而易见的洞察。他很棒。Jason Cohen，你请过 Jason Cohen 上节目吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Jason Cohen, a Smart Bear Jason Cohen?
turns.zh: Jason Cohen，是 Smart Bear 的 Jason Cohen 吗？

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: Yeah, yeah, yeah.
turns.zh: 对对对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: He's coming on the podcast at the end of the year or something.
turns.zh: 他大概年底会来上节目。

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: Oh, that's awesome. What a great plug for him right there.
turns.zh: 哦，太棒了。这给他做了个多好的宣传。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: Yeah, those three would be great. I know they're all men, but.
turns.zh: 对，那三个会很棒。我知道他们都是男的，不过。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Great tips.
turns.zh: 好建议。

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.en: Next question, is there a favorite recent movie or TV show that you've really enjoyed? I know you said you have time to read.
turns.zh: 下一个问题，有没有最近特别喜欢的电影或电视剧？我知道你说过你有时间读书。（玩笑）

turns.en: This is going to be embarrassing, Baywatch.
turns.zh: 这个说出来有点丢人，《海滩救护队》（Baywatch）。

turns.en: Baywatch.
turns.zh: 《海滩救护队》。

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: Yeah. Baywatch channel. It's just so Numby, and it's like '90s classic. Baywatch.
turns.zh: 对。《海滩救护队》频道。就是那么无脑，而且是 90 年代经典。《海滩救护队》。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow, I've never heard that one before. So this is original Baywatch with?
turns.zh: 哇，我以前从没听过这个。所以这是原版《海滩救护队》，有谁？

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: This is original Hasselhoff. David Hasselhoff.
turns.zh: 原版 Hasselhoff。David Hasselhoff。

turns.en: Yeah, Pamela Anderson.
turns.zh: 对，Pamela Anderson。

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: Yasmine Bleeth. Pamela Anderson, the original cast.
turns.zh: Yasmine Bleeth。Pamela Anderson，原班阵容。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing.
turns.zh: 太赞了。

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. Deep cut. Is there a product you recently discovered that you really love?
turns.zh: 好。冷门问题。有没有一个你最近发现、而且真的很喜欢的产品？

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: So the number one thing for me right now is an app called Playground, which is the pictures of my toddler that they upload into the preschool so I can get the daily updates on what's going on in preschool when he's not home.
turns.zh: 所以现在对我来说第一好用的是一款叫 Playground 的 App，就是幼儿园把我小孩的照片传上去，这样当他不在家时，我能每天收到幼儿园里发生什么的更新。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. I need that. We get emails and Google Photos. I would really love that.
turns.zh: 太棒了。我需要这个。我们收到的是邮件和 Google 相册。我真的会喜欢这个。

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: Yeah, there was another one called ClassDojo. There's a few of them, but Playground is the one that this preschool's on.
turns.zh: 对，还有个叫 ClassDojo 的。这类有好几个，但这家幼儿园用的是 Playground。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Love ClassDojo. I'm a small investor.
turns.zh: 喜欢 ClassDojo。我是个小投资人。

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: Are you really?
turns.zh: 真的吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I am.
turns.zh: 我是。

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: Oh, that's awesome.
turns.zh: 哦，太棒了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: How about that? Two more questions. Do you have a favorite life motto that you find yourself coming back to find useful in work or in life?
turns.zh: 怎么样？还有两个问题。你有没有一句最喜欢的人生格言，是你经常回想起、并觉得对工作或生活有用的？

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: Yeah, be direct. Cut the fluff. Give me the bullet, not the paragraph.
turns.zh: 有，要直接。去掉废话。给我要点，不要段落。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Final question. I was told that by Justin that you've never read a sales book. You've just learned to do this. If you were to read a sales book, if there was someone else out there that you look up to, learn from, is there anyone else out there in the world of sales that you most respect?
turns.zh: 最后一个问题。Justin 告诉我，你从没读过一本销售书。你只是自己学会了做这件事。如果你要去读一本销售书，或者如果世界上有你敬佩、想向其学习的人，在销售界还有谁是你最尊重的？

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: I think Jason Lemkin has the strongest understanding of sales. His content is unbelievable. He speaks about it clearly and cleanly, I would say. And as I mentioned, unbelievable Twitter follow. I'm a big fan of his.
turns.zh: 我觉得 Jason Lemkin 对销售的理解最深刻。他的内容令人难以置信。我会说他讲得清晰又干净。而且如我所说，他的 Twitter 值得关注得不得了。我是他的铁粉。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome.
turns.zh: 太棒了。

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: I've actually learned a lot from him too. The 50/50 thing or a higher two salespeople, he's spot on. Failure rate is actually probably higher than 50%.
turns.zh: 其实我也从他身上学了很多。那个 50/50 的事、还有一次招两个销售，他说得完全对。失败率其实可能比 50% 还高。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that guy. And he's so AI-forward these days. He's just building. He almost took down Replit with his complaints. It was a whole new cycle of how Replit-
turns.zh: 我爱那个人。而且他现在对 AI 特别前卫。他就在那儿构建。他差点靠自己的吐槽把 Replit 搞垮。那是关于 Replit 怎么……的一整个新循环——

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: He should interact. Sometimes he says things that are harsh, but you're like, "He's not wrong."
turns.zh: 他应该去互动。有时他说的话很刺耳，但你会想："他没说错。"

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Love it. I got to get him back on the podcast.
turns.zh: 太喜欢了。我得让他再回播客。

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Jen, this was incredible. This was everything I wanted to be. I feel like we just leveled up all the founders that have listened to this in their ability to close. We're going to just create all the economic value and a lot of happy VCs from all the sales that will be closed as a result of the advice you shared. Two final questions. Where can folks find you if they want to either work with you or follow you online? And how can listeners be useful to you?
turns.zh: Jen，这太不可思议了。这正是我想要的样子。我觉得我们刚刚把所有听过这期的创始人在成交能力上都提升了一个档次。因为你的建议，会有一堆交易成交，我们会创造出所有的经济价值，还有一堆开心的 VC。最后两个问题。如果有人想和你合作或在线上关注你，去哪找你？听众怎么帮到你？

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: Twitter. Every new learning or mishap, I put red on Twitter, so it's like my personal diary and super responsive on Twitter DM.
turns.zh: Twitter。每有一个新领悟或失误，我都会发到 Twitter 上，所以它就像我的个人日记，而且在 Twitter DM 上回复超快。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What's your Twitter handle? Twitter handle.
turns.zh: 你的 Twitter 账号是什么？Twitter 账号。

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: It's double J, So J-J-E-N_A-B-E-L.
turns.zh: 是双 J，就是 J-J-E-N_A-B-E-L。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You did not make that easy for people to find you, but we-
turns.zh: 你可没让人们容易找到你，但我们——

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: Yeah, I know, I know, I know I didn't.
turns.zh: 对，我知道，我知道，我知道我没。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And the J is for JJELLYFISH, is that where the extra J is for?
turns.zh: 那个 J 是 JJELLYFISH 的 J 吗，多出来的那个 J 是那个意思？

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: Yeah, the double Js. Then also, well, someone else had the handle, so I was like, "I need my name."
turns.zh: 对，双 J。然后呢，嗯，别人已经占了那个账号，所以我就想："我得用我的名字。"

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it. By the way, just tell people what JJELLYFISH is in case that might be helpful to them.
turns.zh: 明白了。顺便，跟人们说说 JJELLYFISH 是做什么的，也许对他们有帮助。

turns.speaker: Jen Abel
turns.en: Yeah, so it's a consultancy that helps folks in the zero to one stage, and now I'm at general manager of enterprise at State Affairs, which is basically giving citizens and corporations an inside peek into what's actually going on inside the state capitol building. State policy is way more impact than on you, than federal policy. Federal policy is written more about.
